{"id":"KOD-750","uuid":"83a0f426-39e1-4636-9e8b-d6e110a965b7","title":"Ruling: which holder makes the issue-level state moves, and whether the run-event → tracker-state table survives","description":"**Outcome:** the ruling is a dated comment on this issue and the affected criteria are unblocked.
**Fork:** Three rulings pull apart on issue-level state. A8.1 refuses any state write from a session holder and makes the run-event → tracker-state table the only state writer; the 2026-09-01 graph ruling makes a parent's state a rollup and removes the lifecycle writer's terminal write; the lifecycle ruling still has the issue move to In Review on PR open and back to Todo on plateau or budget, and `services/tracker_lifecycle.py` makes exactly those two moves today. Which holder identity makes those two moves, and whether the table survives at all, is unruled. Every refusal that discriminates on who is writing needs the answer — <issue id="d5c63f9e-b4d0-4c1e-b0ea-978caf07dcae" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-390/kod-73-ac-21-four-port-refusals-as-typed-errors-not-prompt-text-parent">KOD-390</issue>'s four refusals, and the write gating on <issue id="7e40ddba-a8ff-4dde-8133-41c1d3936c81" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-386/kod-73-ac-17-writing-a-surface-you-do-not-hold-raises-a-typed-domain">KOD-386</issue>, <issue id="e090613c-f7f1-4e9c-8007-bb8bece4d4ec" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-385/kod-73-ac-16-disjoint-sets-never-contend-two-holders-acquiring">KOD-385</issue> and <issue id="0b99f874-06ed-4239-8e6c-a9be1b125b06" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-383/kod-73-ac-14-a-writable-surface-is-an-addressable-frozen-value-over">KOD-383</issue> that follows <issue id="ebb83291-e57e-4be2-87d6-2b69342a0254" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-747/prevent-a-delayed-claim-renewal-from-reclaiming-ownership-after">KOD-747</issue>'s live demonstration — and <issue id="8d2f80fc-bd12-4cce-84b5-7d6f8599f9ef" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-403/kod-76-ac-7-the-tables-key-set-equals-the-run-event-vocabulary">KOD-403</issue>'s total key-set comparison needs to know whether the table exists.
**Options:** 1. The table is the sole state writer (A8.1's reading): the two lifecycle moves become rows of the table, written under the run's holder, and no lifecycle writer writes an issue state. 2. The lifecycle writer keeps the two issue-level moves under the process (claim) identity and the table covers run events only; session holders refuse, the claim holder does not.
**Pinned interim:** <issue id="d5c63f9e-b4d0-4c1e-b0ea-978caf07dcae" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-390/kod-73-ac-21-four-port-refusals-as-typed-errors-not-prompt-text-parent">KOD-390</issue> refuses only the ruled part; the issue-level move holder is never converted into a blanket refusal of all issue-level moves. Write gating waits on <issue id="ebb83291-e57e-4be2-87d6-2b69342a0254" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-747/prevent-a-delayed-claim-renewal-from-reclaiming-ownership-after">KOD-747</issue>'s live ownership demonstration (founder ruling of 2026-09-08 on <issue id="7e40ddba-a8ff-4dde-8133-41c1d3936c81" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-386/kod-73-ac-17-writing-a-surface-you-do-not-hold-raises-a-typed-domain">KOD-386</issue>).
**Rules:** founder
**Source:** the [decision] comments 0eda4dba (fork 1) and d3626605 on <issue id="65211d3b-bb35-46f7-9ab4-a86577604bb7" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-73/v03-l1-scope-input-scoperef-tracker-port-container-vocabulary">KOD-73</issue>; 8921c674 on <issue id="d5c63f9e-b4d0-4c1e-b0ea-978caf07dcae" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-390/kod-73-ac-21-four-port-refusals-as-typed-errors-not-prompt-text-parent">KOD-390</issue>; 0964acf0 on <issue id="7e40ddba-a8ff-4dde-8133-41c1d3936c81" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-386/kod-73-ac-17-writing-a-surface-you-do-not-hold-raises-a-typed-domain">KOD-386</issue>; 5f2a366e on <issue id="0b99f874-06ed-4239-8e6c-a9be1b125b06" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-383/kod-73-ac-14-a-writable-surface-is-an-addressable-frozen-value-over">KOD-383</issue>; 2fba6877 on <issue id="e090613c-f7f1-4e9c-8007-bb8bece4d4ec" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-385/kod-73-ac-16-disjoint-sets-never-contend-two-holders-acquiring">KOD-385</issue>; the fork note in aa60c73b on <issue id="c2ab66ca-a97a-4ba3-9883-d06b76878ab6" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-76/v03-l4-tracker-as-live-run-state-evaluator-write-back-validation-from">KOD-76</issue> (<issue id="8d2f80fc-bd12-4cce-84b5-7d6f8599f9ef" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-403/kod-76-ac-7-the-tables-key-set-equals-the-run-event-vocabulary">KOD-403</issue>).

{"id":"KOD-751","uuid":"49dff0c9-44ec-4399-b1fc-3af0d70752f7","title":"Ruling: who owns the approval barrier that refuses a scope holding an open decision or a Backlog criterion","description":"**Outcome:** the ruling is a dated comment on this issue and the affected criteria are unblocked.
**Fork:** The 2026-09-01 ruling names the port lane (<issue id="65211d3b-bb35-46f7-9ab4-a86577604bb7" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-73/v03-l1-scope-input-scoperef-tracker-port-container-vocabulary">KOD-73</issue>) owner of the approval barrier — `scope:approved` is refused, typed, with the offending keys named, while the scope holds an open `decision` or a Backlog criterion. No deliverable or criterion on <issue id="65211d3b-bb35-46f7-9ab4-a86577604bb7" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-73/v03-l1-scope-input-scoperef-tracker-port-container-vocabulary">KOD-73</issue> covers it, and minting one is ORGANIZE's or the founder's act, not a writer's. Meanwhile the plan-time refusal (a typed refusal naming open decisions, Backlog criteria and crossing edges) has been implemented on the walker lane under <issue id="851175ee-fc1e-4d64-8191-8b85cd744243" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-450/kod-75-ac-15-plan-time-refusal-holds-the-walk-and-every-fire-re">KOD-450</issue>. One barrier, two candidate owners, and nothing on the board says which criterion the approval-time half belongs to.
**Options:** 1. The barrier is the walker lane's plan-time refusal (<issue id="851175ee-fc1e-4d64-8191-8b85cd744243" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-450/kod-75-ac-15-plan-time-refusal-holds-the-walk-and-every-fire-re">KOD-450</issue>); <issue id="65211d3b-bb35-46f7-9ab4-a86577604bb7" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-73/v03-l1-scope-input-scoperef-tracker-port-container-vocabulary">KOD-73</issue> mints no criterion and its Fix points at <issue id="851175ee-fc1e-4d64-8191-8b85cd744243" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-450/kod-75-ac-15-plan-time-refusal-holds-the-walk-and-every-fire-re">KOD-450</issue>. 2. <issue id="65211d3b-bb35-46f7-9ab4-a86577604bb7" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-73/v03-l1-scope-input-scoperef-tracker-port-container-vocabulary">KOD-73</issue> mints a criterion for the approval-time refusal at the port (the `scope:approved` write itself refused while the scope holds an open decision or a Backlog criterion), and the walker's plan-time refusal remains a second, later check.
**Pinned interim:** nothing is built on <issue id="65211d3b-bb35-46f7-9ab4-a86577604bb7" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-73/v03-l1-scope-input-scoperef-tracker-port-container-vocabulary">KOD-73</issue>; the walker's plan-time refusal stands as the only barrier.
**Rules:** ORGANIZE pass (the founder may rule sooner)
**Source:** the [decision] comment 0eda4dba (fork 2) on <issue id="65211d3b-bb35-46f7-9ab4-a86577604bb7" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-73/v03-l1-scope-input-scoperef-tracker-port-container-vocabulary">KOD-73</issue>; the [ruling] 69978aaa on <issue id="3abe7693-0e37-47a2-ab02-026d28f029df" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-74/v03-l2-organize-node-the-spec-pass-as-a-graph-step-make-everything-in">KOD-74</issue> (approval barrier row); the code-grounded grooming comment 623584fc on <issue id="851175ee-fc1e-4d64-8191-8b85cd744243" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-450/kod-75-ac-15-plan-time-refusal-holds-the-walk-and-every-fire-re">KOD-450</issue>.

{"comments":[{"id":"763f4f9e-6e3a-4bb2-b3f8-ffeff8b53016","body":"[recovery execution boundary · 2026-09-12 · fresh Linear contract read]

The latest operative discussion is reopening/refutation 74001c73-67ab-41de-a258-fd3bb9c8e7d9. Earlier Option 1 comment 28a90b81-8d19-4c86-9051-1874a832939b cannot be treated as a settled approval-barrier ruling: the cited founder table names KOD-73 as owner.

The exact unresolved work is ownership and acceptance coverage of the approval-time refusal, versus KOD-450's existing plan-time refusal. An ORGANIZE pass may rederive an interpretation from source authority that actually supports it; otherwise founder resolution is needed. This is narrower than blocking all L1/L3 work. Existing plan-time refusal remains the pinned interim, while native in-memory execution, class removal and HTTP typing continue independently. No criterion or state is changed by this checkpoint.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-09-12T11:16:56.306Z","updatedAt":"2026-09-12T11:16:56.277Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"74001c73-67ab-41de-a258-fd3bb9c8e7d9","body":"[audit 2026-09-08 · workhorse tier, provisional] reopened: GROUND — the ruling's own cited ground contradicts it. 15526c96 (founder, 2026-09-01), row "no assumptions reach the workhorse", reads: "every fork ORGANIZE cannot settle is a `decision` on the issue, and the approval barrier refuses a scope with an open `decision` or a Backlog criterion in it", and its Owner column reads verbatim "ORGANIZE (KOD-74) · approval barrier (KOD-73)". The ground names KOD-73 as the owner of the approval barrier. The ruling concludes the opposite — "KOD-73 mints no criterion for an approval-time refusal … KOD-73 owes nothing here" — only by reinterpreting that owner ("the 'approval barrier (KOD-73)' owner in 15526c96 resolves to the port's read of the approval label … not to a criterion of its own"). That is the ruling's paraphrase, not the ground's words: 15526c96 names an owner of a rule, and reading an owner out of the table is not a reading the ground supports. Fork 2 of 0eda4dba on KOD-73 stands open; the fork is founder-owned or must be re-argued from a ground that does not name KOD-73 as owner.

Two of three independent refuters rejected this ruling; provisional pending top-tier re-verification. State returned to Todo. No criterion Check changed under this ruling, so nothing is restored.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-09-08T20:48:46.169Z","updatedAt":"2026-09-08T20:48:46.129Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"28a90b81-8d19-4c86-9051-1874a832939b","body":"[ruling 2026-09-08 · ORGANIZE pass] Option 1. The approval barrier is the walker lane's plan-time refusal (KOD-450): the machine reads `scope:approved` and refuses to begin the walk while the scope holds an open `decision`, a Backlog criterion or a crossing leaf edge, naming the keys. KOD-73 mints no criterion for an approval-time refusal: `scope:approved` is the one human act (5a59ce38, 7e3f8808) set on the vendor's surface, and the port never writes the approval member itself (KOD-390 clause 3 refuses a run-holder label write naming it; `core/protocols.py:846-852` at 8257113 — "label presence decides; there is no approval-actor carrier"), so there is no port write path on which a second refusal could sit. The "approval barrier (KOD-73)" owner in 15526c96 resolves to the port's read of the approval label that feeds the planner's refusal, not to a criterion of its own. — ground: 5a59ce38 (stage markers vs approval row), 7e3f8808 (ORGANIZE exit), 15526c96 (no assumptions reach the workhorse), 69978aaa (approval barrier row); measured: `services/scope_planning.py:44-71` at 8257113 raises `ScopePlanRefusalError` naming open decisions, Backlog criteria and cross-subtree edges (grooming comment 623584fc on KOD-450: clause 1 met); KOD-744 forbids a second mechanism for a behaviour one site already owns. consequence: no criterion changes; KOD-450's Check stands as the only barrier; fork 2 of 0eda4dba on KOD-73 is closed and KOD-73 owes nothing here.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-09-08T17:31:09.378Z","updatedAt":"2026-09-08T17:31:09.341Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null}],"hasNextPage":false}

{"id":"KOD-787","uuid":"4bdd27fc-9471-4bb7-9e69-17e25efe931f","title":"Ruling: where scope approval is established, and how an unapproved member is made legible","description":"**Outcome:** the ruling is a dated comment on this issue and the affected criterion is unblocked.
**Fork:** <issue id="45ffebde-e6c3-43cc-9ab5-e78fc0be641b" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-451/kod-75-ac-16-the-dispatch-target-is-the-issue-itself-no-marker-is">KOD-451</issue> requires an issue outside the approved scope to be "refused at plan time rather than reaching the walk". <issue id="d2b3ac56-8fc2-42c7-b5b4-95f6077d1d6e" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-425/kod-75-ac-3-a-lane-is-ready-iff-it-is-approved-and-every-in-scope">KOD-425</issue>'s Do puts the `scope:approved` self-or-ancestor cascade inside the READY predicate in chains/scope_walker.py, and services/scope_planning.py states as its contract that it establishes no approval and leaves it to the walker. Measured at 8257113: `execution_approved` is read in chains/scope_walker.py and nowhere else in src; the two-root container with only the first root approved dispatches the approved one and drops the other with `exclusions == []`, no clause and no log; and a wholly unapproved scope returns outcome empty_eligible_set with empty eligible, exclusions and snapshot — a report that compares EQUAL to the same scope with every criterion met. "Not approved" is today indistinguishable from "nothing to do".
**Options:** 1. Approval stays walker-owned as <issue id="d2b3ac56-8fc2-42c7-b5b4-95f6077d1d6e" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-425/kod-75-ac-3-a-lane-is-ready-iff-it-is-approved-and-every-in-scope">KOD-425</issue> pins it; <issue id="45ffebde-e6c3-43cc-9ab5-e78fc0be641b" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-451/kod-75-ac-16-the-dispatch-target-is-the-issue-itself-no-marker-is">KOD-451</issue>'s clause is read as "never reaches dispatch", and the walker records each unapproved member as an exclusion under the existing ExclusionClause.NOT_APPROVED and logs it, so an unapproved scope is legible as such. 2. Approval moves to plan time: read_scope_plan establishes the cascade and refuses, typed, naming the unapproved keys, so an unapproved member never reaches the walk — <issue id="d2b3ac56-8fc2-42c7-b5b4-95f6077d1d6e" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-425/kod-75-ac-3-a-lane-is-ready-iff-it-is-approved-and-every-in-scope">KOD-425</issue>'s Do is amended, and the partially-approved container is ruled with it (refuse the whole plan, or plan over the approved members only). 3. Split: the plan reader establishes the cascade as a fact on the snapshot without refusing, the walker excludes under NOT_APPROVED, and a refusal is raised only when no member of the scope is approved.
**Pinned interim:** the shipped behaviour — approval read in the walk, unapproved members silently absent. No code moves on <issue id="45ffebde-e6c3-43cc-9ab5-e78fc0be641b" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-451/kod-75-ac-16-the-dispatch-target-is-the-issue-itself-no-marker-is">KOD-451</issue> until this is ruled.
**Rules:** founder

* that a value the tracker already answers is cheaper read than judged;
* that ownership arbitration cannot be a session, because a session asked whether it holds an issue may answer yes twice (<issue id="ebb83291-e57e-4be2-87d6-2b69342a0254" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-747/prevent-a-delayed-claim-renewal-from-reclaiming-ownership-after">KOD-747</issue>);

* that anything an audit must reproduce identically has to be arithmetic, or two runs cannot be compared.

**Run-event → tracker-state table.** Current trunk models it in `OperationConfig` and validates totality/effects, but `TrackerLifecycleWriter` still bypasses it with direct stage writes. KOD-750 has already ruled the table the sole issue-state writer, so the architectural defect is *two authorities*, not merely table complexity. A session could judge what happened, but it cannot replace the deterministic requirement that the same typed event maps to the same tracker transition across adapters/replays. If retained, keep one configured total table and one port-bound applier; remove the parallel lifecycle writer. KOD-797 remains a real representability decision for restore-to-preclaim/budget semantics.

**`domain/dispatch.py::select_top_ranked`.** It computes the operator-declared ordering (domain priority, oldest first, injected draw only on exact equality) and reports the tied set. A session could choose an issue, but replacing this function would lose reproducibility of an explicit scheduling policy and make two identical tracker snapshots legally produce unexplained different priorities. This reads as deterministic policy rather than semantic judgment; if the founder wants agent selection, the ranking contract itself should be retired/amended rather than silently delegated.

**Dispatch clauses inspected.** `clause_in_team`, `clause_in_scope`, `clause_recorded_repository`, `clause_approved`, `clause_open`, `live_blocker`, `clause_unclaimed`, and `clause_undelivered` are direct predicates over port-returned/configured facts. They do not attempt semantic interpretation. Replacing these with a session would trade testable boundary predicates for judgment without adding information. One caveat is approval: the *placement/legibility* policy around scope approval is still open on KOD-787/KOD-751; that decision can change which fact is evaluated where, but it does not make the fact itself semantic.

**`domain/topology.py::plan_topology`.** Pure graph arithmetic: validates complete blocker facts, rejects cycles/missing nodes, propagates effective priority through the blockedBy DAG, and returns ready/blocked sets. A session could propose an order but would lose the equality between the declared blocker graph and the computed ready set, and would make cycle/missing-fact refusal probabilistic. This is a strong example of a deterministic component encoding a fact/policy rather than standing in for a model call.

**`domain/issue_tree.py`.** `index_issue_tree` is structural validation; `SubtreeClosure` defines the gap as the still-open criterion records throughout the subtree; `EmptyFireCriteriaError` refuses a deliverable with no criterion family; `ScopeSupersessionReadError` refuses canceled/duplicate criteria when no native supersession reference is available. The tree/closure arithmetic is reproducible tracker-state interpretation. The *meaning* of whether a criterion is satisfiable belongs in a session; membership/parentage/state/supersession-reference completeness do not.

**Observed counterexample to “agent call over any deterministic component” as a mechanical rewrite rule.** The same review found PR112/PR115 doing the opposite mistake: semantic amendment grounds such as “unsatisfiable at base” are approximated by path/substring/quote mechanics. Those should move toward a structured agent judgment with deterministic evidence/postvalidation. Conversely, topology, ownership, identity, event mapping, exact roster equality, and tracker-native state reads are facts whose reproducibility is part of their contract. The useful cut is therefore not `agent vs code` globally; it is **semantic judgment → typed agent call, invariant/fact/policy arithmetic → deterministic code**. Founder still decides whether that interpretation satisfies the 2026-09-09 KISS ruling.

**DRY/SOLID/hexagonal observations from the initiative review:** current risk is duplicated authority: direct lifecycle writes alongside the event table; `DeliveryCoordinator` name used for union verification while L5 expects a different landing coordinator; `LaneReport` readback shape standing near but not equal to the L6 delivery vector; scope walker implementation not selected by composition. The healing plan should remove/rename these competing authorities before adding new abstractions.

The defect was the tie-break being applied to a holder's own second grant: each retracted the other's marker, so the pair annihilated. A holder identity is exactly what the arbitration is over, so a second grant to it is the same ownership observed twice rather than a conflict to break. `domain/surface_lease.one_ownership` states the rule once — the grant the backend ordered FIRST stands for both and every later one withdraws INTO it — and earliest rather than latest because the two sides do not see one log: the earlier marker is already there when the later one reads back, while the later one's may not be there when the earlier reads, so only the earliest is a choice both sides reach from what each can see. A grant of the holder's that has LAPSED never stands there, so a restart cleans its predecessor's marker up instead of inheriting it; and a grant withdrawing into another carries it forward through the same fenced renewal every renewal uses, so one that lapsed while its successor was standing down renews nothing and the address stays with whoever took it. The in-memory tracker had restated the same rule inline on its claim side and had it the other way round (a holder was refused its own live claim); it now decides by the function its own lease side already decided by.

Second finding, measured on the real board and pinned rather than assumed (14268d9): when the log hid each grant's confirmation from the other's read-back, BOTH stood and two markers of ONE holder were left. That is a duplicate and not a second owner — every reader names the same holder, a rival is refused in that name, the renewal carries, and the marker nothing renews lapses — so it is left to lapse rather than compensated for by deleting a marker another live grant of this holder may still be reading.

Founder's words:

> *"in the ralph loop it's gonna launch dynamic workflows but within one approved scope and each scope is a queue item"*
> *"if one agent is working on a lane just mark it as scope:in_progress or something and be done with it idk??"*
> *"like the agent working on this will know and a lane is always a parent issue"*

**The three levels this settles, which had been collapsed into one question:**
1. **A scope is a queue item.** Scopes are serial — the queue holds them one at a time.
2. **Lanes inside a scope may run concurrently.** A mark on the lane is what keeps two agents off the same one. A lane is always a parent issue, so the mark has exactly one place to live.
3. **Inside one lane's run, the loop launches dynamic workflows.** One operator, one process — never in question and never the problem.

**What this replaces.** Marker-comment arbitration with leases, expiry, renewal, fences and clock arithmetic. Four repair rounds against it were each refuted, and two of them left an issue owned by nobody with no collision present. It is not repaired, it is retired.

**Half of it is already built, verified in the code today at trunk `38a7b14`:**
- `services/tracker_lifecycle.py::on_dequeue` already does `set_workflow_state(stage=LifecycleStage.IN_PROGRESS)` — its docstring reads *"The run started: move the issue to its in-progress state."* **kodezart already raises the flag.**
- Nothing reads it. `domain/dispatch.py::clause_unclaimed` is `claim is None and not run_is_live` — the marker, and an in-memory register that dies with the process. Neither is the issue's state. And `clause_open` admits a started issue, because `is_open` excludes only completed, canceled and duplicate.

So the change is: **read the flag instead of the marker.**

**Two properties of this the founder should have on the record, since they are consequences and not decisions.** The window moves rather than closing — the mark is written when the run starts, after selection, so two walkers in that gap both see it unmarked; the difference is that losing that race costs one wasted run and contains no clock. And a crashed run leaves the mark stuck on, which the grooming pass already owns as exactly the kind of state drift it reconciles.

**Open sub-question this does NOT settle** — the founder said "or something idk", explicitly delegating the carrier: is the mark the existing workflow state (already written by `on_dequeue`, no new vocabulary) or a new `scope:in_progress` label beside `scope:approved`? Both satisfy the ruling.

**Board contradiction this resolves:** KOD-75's body says the walker *"dispatches one execution-only fire at a time"* and *"one fire per pass"*; the v0.3 initiative says *"for each READY lane (concurrency from config)"* and its worked example *"roots = {A, C} → fire BOTH in parallel"*. The ruling is with the initiative — lanes may be concurrent, serialised per lane by the mark. Round four was refuted, making four consecutive. Rather than a fifth repair, five questions were put to fifteen agents in fresh context — each given every measurement the four rounds produced, and deliberately not given the shape of any of the four designs. Five more counted the votes. **This issue blocks 76 others, so the finding matters; it decides nothing.**

**Unanimous, fifteen of fifteen, on what the four rounds are evidence of:** not an intrinsically hard problem, but one shared wrong assumption attacked four times — that the record of who owns an issue had to live on the tracker and be arbitrated there. The tracker offers no conditional write. Two of the measurements make that family unsalvageable: a comment creation was observed taking **45.5 seconds** to land, and with a tail that long *"your ownership expired"* and *"your write has not landed yet"* are the same observation arriving through the same channel, indistinguishable.

**Ruled out by construction, verified independently.** A hung tick cannot overlap the next — the scheduler is strictly serial and cancels rather than abandons. A crash cannot leave a run behind — the queue lives in the process and dies with it; what survives is a stale note that *delays* re-dispatch, which is slowness, not duplication.

**What a collision actually costs, traced through the code.** Two branches that cannot clash (random component in the name, nothing force-pushes). Two pull requests, both stopping at a human — nothing auto-merges. Duplicate comments. One wasted run. Blast radius capped at two, because an open pull request excludes the issue everywhere. The only damage that spreads beyond the colliding issue is the delivering-branch record: first writer wins and the loser's conflict is swallowed and only logged.

**Unanimous verdict on proportionality:** the cost of a collision is not proportionate to the cost of preventing it. Two of the four rounds left an issue owned by nobody and let an unrelated holder take it — *with no collision present.* The prevention has produced worse outcomes than the thing prevented.

**On the founder's KISS ruling, fifteen of fifteen, none reflexively:** it does not apply to the exclusion itself. "Is another copy running this issue?" is arithmetic over a register the process already holds, and an agent asked it faces the same missing information plus unpredictability. All fifteen placed the agent call one step over, in the same place — judging whether a started issue with no live run and no open PR is abandoned, deciding what becomes of a half-written branch, choosing which of two pull requests delivers.

Three findings this produced are filed separately: KOD-807, KOD-808, KOD-809.

**Open questions for the founder,** stated as questions: how many copies are meant to run at once, today and against the real repositories; whether anything actually uses the manual fire endpoint; whether two pull requests and one wasted run is an acceptable failure or unacceptable regardless of cost; whether a crashed issue should park for up to fifteen minutes or retry immediately at the risk of duplication; what becomes of a dead run's branch; and how much more this is worth spending on at all.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-09-09T08:27:19.202Z","updatedAt":"2026-09-09T08:27:19.163Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"d79cb6d0-4273-4346-b1fc-3232a1872712","body":"**[live measurement 2026-09-09]** — round four, branch `kodezart/v03-live-ownership` @ `1e69845`, probe issue KOD-780, two MCP sessions, 8 cases green. What each round measured, at the same seam:

- **Round one (judged 2026-09-08, over the fake MCP server through the real adapter).** The shipped renewal was write-then-compensate, not fenced: `adapters/linear_mcp_tracker.py` edited the holder's own earliest marker with the new expiry and only afterwards asked whether the lease had lapsed, then deleted. Measured: a stale holder's extension reaches the board before it learns it lost, and the new holder's exclusivity rests on a compensating delete the vendor cannot bind to the write (an unretried `_delete_markers` loop). A reader placed between the edit and the delete read runner-a while runner-b held.
- **Round two (re-judged 2026-09-08, same harness).** The repair made the extension state the expiry it replaces and had readers hold it to that deadline "in the backend's clock", converting with `created_at` − `granted_at` off the marker's own creation. Measured: that difference is not a clock offset — it is the offset PLUS however long the create took to land. Lease 60s, skew 0.5s, A's create landing 5s late: A lapses, B is GRANTED, and A's extension lands inside a fence deadline inflated by exactly the create latency, so the lapsed holder's extension is in force and two holders own the issue.
- **Round three (judged 2026-09-09, same harness, head e1953f5).** The repair moved to durations plus backend-supplied instants, removing the conversion. Measured instead, with no injected fault, no veiled read and no slow write: two `LinearMcpTracker` instances over one fake server (skew +1.25s), lease 45s, both claiming FIX-1 for ONE holder identity, gathered — both return GRANTED, `delete_comment` fires for both markers, ZERO markers stand, `active_claim` is None, a third holder is then GRANTED the same issue, and the original holder's `renew_claim` returns None. Deterministic 5/5, and again under pytest-randomly. Gate reproduced (9051 passed / 24 skipped, exit 0) and the live probe reproduced green on a quiet board, so the failure is in the arbitration, not the environment.

The through-line across all three: each round closes the conversion or compensation the previous round was refuted on, and the next refutation lands on the fact that the vendor offers no compare-and-swap, no expected-version field and no caller-chosen id — every marker is an independent request, so a decision is never bound to the write that publishes it. The bid-then-confirm construction of round three is the closest attempt yet and still admits a duplicate-identity replay that leaves the address unowned.

Recommended: put to the founder whether "B remains the sole owner / replay never creates a second effective owner" is achievable against this backend's real capabilities, or whether the criterion needs restating against what the vendor can actually guarantee (for example, at-most-one-effective-owner among *distinct* identities, with replay of a single identity handled at the runner rather than the board).","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-09-09T00:36:50.590Z","updatedAt":"2026-09-09T00:36:50.539Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"9c478a40-11dd-4ae8-baba-6d783cee6751","body":"**[live measurement 2026-09-09]** — branch `kodezart/v03-live-ownership` @ `a1258c0`, run `cddf2ae0`, probe issue KOD-780, two MCP sessions, `pytest -m live tests/probes/test_live_ownership.py` → 7 passed in 189.83s. The rows below replace the earlier live block: those predate both fences and no longer describe the code.

| question | configuration | observed | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| is comment creation order server-assigned and stable? | 8 markers, 3 read-backs | distinct instants 8/8; identical order 3/3; monotonic vs write order True; fractional digits [2,3]; skew +0.278s..+0.881s | stable |
| does an edit keep a comment's place and move its stamp? | one comment, one edit by id | createdAt kept True; updatedAt moved True by +2.693s; creation to first update −0.012s | orderable |
| **does a grant whose creation lands late gain fence immunity?** | creation delayed 7s, lease 60s, renewal landed inside the window the refuted arithmetic would have granted | creation landed **+7.574s** after the call began; replacement GRANTED; renewal **+6.197s past the deadline** (immunity window 7s) → **None**; active claim = B; markers standing 1 | **no immunity** |
| can a renewal delayed past its expiry take the issue back? | lease 60s, waited past it, other holder claimed | replacement granted; stale renewal None; active claim = B; markers standing 1 | no restore |
| do two simultaneous claimants produce exactly one owner? | two sessions, lease 120s | granted [B]; refused [(contended, None)]; active claim B; 1 marker | one owner |
| does a lease exclude an intersecting set and admit a disjoint one? | description + two marker comments | intersecting refused naming A; disjoint granted to B | exclusive |
| does a release hand the surfaces and the issue on? | release then acquire, release then claim | inherited by B; claim after release granted; active claim after release None | freed |
| does the run leave the probe issue as it found it? | run cddf2ae0 | **swept 0; remaining 0** | clean |

**The row that matters.** The renewal was landed deliberately inside the window the refuted arithmetic would have made immune: 6.197s past the deadline the creation bought, against a create latency of 7.574s that the old fence read as a clock offset. It renewed nothing, B stayed sole owner, and one marker stood. The board was left exactly as found — the sweep found nothing to remove and nothing remaining, so **the probe left no marker behind**.

**Decision recorded, for the founder rather than as a weaker implementation.** The hypothesis offered — an extension as its own APPENDED marker, so a grant is a chain folded from server instants — was tested and rejected, on cost and on soundness of pruning, not on ordering. Ordering is total enough: measured 8/8 distinct, stable across 3 read-backs, monotonic against write order. What fails is pruning. Link *n*'s validity needs its predecessor's stamp AND the duration that predecessor bought, and the port takes a lease duration per call, so the cumulative deadline cannot be reconstructed from the anchor and a sequence number. **Reproduced first.** Over the fake MCP server, with the Check's own interleaving: a reader placed between the delayed extension's write and the delete compensating for it read `runner-a` as the owner while `runner-b` held the issue. With that delete refused by the backend, the lapsed holder's marker stayed on the board — earliest in order, stating a live expiry — and `runner-a` read as the owner for good, while the renewal raised the transport failure instead of reporting lost ownership.

**What changed at `8e7e055`.** An extension now states the expiry it replaces, and every reader holds it to that deadline. The two stamps the backend assigns are the fence: `createdAt`, which the order rests on, and the `updatedAt` an edit moves. They are the backend's clock and the expiries are the holder's — so the comparison is made in the backend's, converted per marker by the two readings the marker's own creation carries (`granted-at` beside `createdAt`). That is what the original design's "created after own previous expiry" clause wanted and what the shipped implementation had backed away from as a cross-clock comparison: measured per marker, the offset makes clocks any distance apart decide identically, which the fixture's two-month gap now demonstrates directly.

An edit the backend stamps after the grant it extends had lapsed therefore puts nothing in force: the marker keeps the expiry it had. The holder that took the address meanwhile is the sole owner from the moment it acquired, and stays so whether or not the lapsed holder's withdrawal ever reaches the board. The lapsed holder still takes its marker down — litter nobody else may remove — but nothing rests on it any more.

**Second change, the same class.** A withdrawal no longer stops at the first marker the backend refuses; it attempts every one. And a withdrawal that compensates for a decided outcome is recorded (`tracker_withdrawal_incomplete`, naming what stayed) rather than raised: a holder told it holds nothing is told that, not handed a transport failure. A release is the caller's own request rather than compensation, so it still raises — a holder told its release succeeded would stop renewing a grant that is still standing.

**Live measurement re-read, not re-run.** The fence rests on a property already measured on this board and recorded above: an update by comment id replaces the body and moves `updatedAt` while `createdAt` is preserved, and the skew between the backend's stamp and the writing holder's clock was +0.352s..+0.613s — three orders of magnitude below any lease. The probe should be re-run against this tip before the criterion is closed.

The refusing acquisition/renewal arms, the two unsupported-capability errors, the heartbeat's permanent-refusal branch and the conformance suite's refusal wrapper are gone. Claims and surface leases are one mechanism built on the design comment above: a marker per grant per target carrying kind, holder, per-grant nonce, expiry and the whole address set; create, read every target back, and keep the grant only where no other holder's live marker over a requested address was created no later than own. Strictly earlier reports the owner; an equal instant reports a tie and BOTH sides withdraw. A holder that cannot find its own marker in the read-back withdraws and raises rather than claiming a grant it could not verify. The set arithmetic stays one function, generalised over the address type, so the in-memory double and the adapter decide contention identically.

**One deviation from the design, and why.** The design's renewal read-back clause was "no other live grant created after own PREVIOUS expiry". That compares a server timestamp against a holder wall clock, and the ruling above says timestamp order is never trusted blindly — this comparison is exactly the kind that a clock offset makes meaningless (in the conformance fixture the two clocks sit two months apart, so the clause would never fire and the counterexample would pass unnoticed). The implemented rule stays inside one clock and is strictly stronger for the same counterexample: after the edit lands, the holder compares **its own clock** against the expiry it HAD. A lease that lapsed while the write was in flight is handed back with its marker, whoever took the issue meanwhile. A holder still inside its previous lease keeps its place, so a competitor that arrives and loses cannot cost a working run its claim.

Conformance now runs identical assertions over both implementations — `TestAtomicClaim` (10 × 2), `TestRenewingAClaim` (7 × 2), `TestSurfaceLease` (18 × 2). `tests/tracker/test_ownership_arbitration.py` adds what a serial caller cannot produce, over the fake MCP server: two holders that both wrote before either read back at one instant (both contended, no marker left, and the issue reads unclaimed while both markers stand), the delayed renewal across an expiry the issue changed hands over (renewal returns nothing, the new holder is sole owner, one marker on the log), a creation the log does not answer with (typed protocol refusal, nothing left), a restarted holder pruning its own predecessor, and a renewal that edits by id and preserves the creation instant.

Plan for the live-ownership wave. Designed against the ruling above and the reply on KOD-386's decision thread: the shipped adapter implements claims AND surface leases on what the vendor actually provides, and proves it on the real board. Nothing here touches code; it is the brief the implementer builds from.

**1. What the vendor provides, and what the design leans on**

Measured on this board (KOD-96 mapping proof 2026-08-08; v0.2 finale): comment creation is append-only with a server-assigned `createdAt`; a listing read after a write contains that write; an update by comment id replaces the body and moves only `updatedAt` (`createdAt` is preserved); deletion by id; comments can be parented on an issue, a project, an initiative or a milestone. NOT provided: compare-and-swap, an expected-version field, a caller-chosen creation id. So every decision is made by **verify-after-write**: a holder writes, re-reads the live marker set, and keeps its grant only if the read-back says it is the earliest live grant for every address it asked for. Timestamp order is never trusted from the write echo; it is re-read, and a holder that is not earliest withdraws its own marker.

**2. The marker (one per grant per target)**

One comment per grant, parented on the target the surface addresses (the issue for issue surfaces and claims; the project/initiative/milestone for container surfaces). A grant over surfaces on several targets writes one marker on each target, all carrying the same nonce, in the canonical address order (`domain/surface_lease._address`) so two holders racing on one set write in the same order. Body is a fenced block with an info string — the 2026-08-12 finding on KOD-96 measured code formatting as the form this vendor cannot transform (bare ids were auto-linkified); the info string carries the operation's configured marker prefix for the `claim` purpose, so readers and writers share the same mapping as today's `LinearMarkers`:

```
kind: claim | lease
holder: <process identity for a claim, job id for a lease>
nonce: <per-grant uuid4 hex>
granted-at: <holder wall clock at the write, ISO-8601 UTC>
expires-at: <ISO-8601 UTC>
surfaces: one canonical address per line (kind, ref kind, ref key, marker)
```

`nonce` identifies a holder's OWN markers on read-back independent of the holder string, so a restarted deployment carrying the same holder finds its predecessor's marker as a duplicate of its own and prunes it, never as a competitor. The v0.2 HTML-comment claim form is not read (no compat reader); any such marker still on a board is expired.

**3. Arbitration — one function, both vocabularies**

Adapter-private `_Grant(kind, holder, nonce, addresses, created_at per target, expires_at, comment id per target)`; three private operations `_grant`, `_extend`, `_withdraw` and one reader `_live_grants(kind, targets)`. `claim_issue` is `_grant(kind=claim, addresses={issue})` mapped to `ClaimResult`; `acquire_surfaces` is `_grant(kind=lease, addresses=surfaces)` mapped to `SurfaceLease` / `SurfaceLeaseError`. Kinds never intersect (KOD-388 stays true by construction). The set arithmetic is `domain/surface_lease.live_conflict`, generalised over the address type (the fake keeps calling it unchanged with its serial registry); the shipped adapter feeds it `held` = the other holders' live grants whose marker on the contested target was created **no later than** own (`created_at <= own created_at`). No second arithmetic.

*Acquire.* Create own marker(s) → read back every live marker on every target → GRANTED only if no other live grant intersecting a requested address has `created_at <= own` on that target. Strictly earlier: withdraw (delete own markers by id) and report LOST / raise `SurfaceLeaseError` naming the surface and the earliest holder. **Equal `createdAt`: withdraw and report CONTENDED naming the tying holder — never GRANTED.** A holder that was granted earlier had no tie at its own read-back and keeps its grant; only two holders still mid-decision both back off, which leaves nobody holding and both retrying on their next pass. Own marker absent from its read-back: delete by id, raise `TrackerProtocolError` (a grant that cannot be verified is not a grant). `ClaimStatus` gains `CONTENDED`; `ClaimResult` gains `current_holder: str | None` (the holder whose marker outranks or ties); the dispatcher routes on `is not GRANTED` and keeps `DispatchOutcome.claim_lost` for both.

*Renew.* Read first: own grant (by nonce) must be live by wall clock AND earliest for every own address; otherwise delete own, return `None` — the port's LOST report — logging the holder now earliest. Then update the marker body by id with `expires_at = max(now + lease, current)`. Then read back: own marker carries the written expiry, is still earliest, and no other live grant on an own address was created after own PREVIOUS expiry (a grant minted while own lease had lapsed between the read and the update landing). Any of those failing: delete own, return `None`, extend nothing. Counterexample (1) is decided at the first read: A's marker is expired, so A never writes.

*Release.* Delete every marker of (kind, holder) on the targets; idempotent; a non-holder deletes nothing. *Reader* (`active_claim`): earliest live claim marker; two live claim markers with equal `createdAt` from distinct holders is "nobody confirmed" → `None`. *Expiry*: reader wall clock vs `expires-at`; expired markers are dead and ignored; a holder only ever deletes its own (nonce or holder+kind) markers.

*Clocks.* Order is server time; expiry is holder wall clock, as in v0.2. The one cross-clock comparison (renewal's "created after own previous expiry") tolerates skew far below the lease (minutes); the probe measures `createdAt − local write instant` and records it.

**4. What stays exactly as defined**

Port signatures and semantics in `core/protocols.py` are unchanged (keyword-only; `LOST` is a value; renew returns `None` when not held; acquisition all-or-nothing and never blocks; `SurfaceLeaseError` carries surface and current holder). `tests/tracker/test_tracker_conformance.py` stays parameterised over `[fake-port]` and `[linear-mcp]` and BOTH must pass every row of `TestAtomicClaim`, `TestRenewingAClaim`, `TestSurfaceLease` on the same fixture workspace; the `refusal_contract` wrapper, its self-test, `UnsupportedClaimError`/`UnsupportedLeaseError`, the heartbeat's refusal branch and `tests/tracker/test_claim_capability.py` / `test_lease_capability.py` go — replaced by adapter-level tests over the fake MCP server: the tie (`comment_instants` repeated → both CONTENDED, no marker left), the delayed-renewal interleaving kept as a positive assertion, own-marker-missing, container-parented markers. Lease durations stay the existing `tracker_claim_lease_seconds` / `tracker_surface_lease_seconds` / `tracker_claim_renewal_fraction`; no new setting.

**5. Live probe** — `tests/probes/test_live_ownership.py`, marker `live`, dialled through `composition.tracker.boot_tracker` from the operator's `.env` (nested names; step 0 migrates them). Targets ONLY the issue titled "kodezart live probe — ownership arbitration" on the kodezart board (found by title, created once if absent); never any other issue. Two adapter instances over two MCP sessions. (a) create 8 markers back to back, read back three times: assert identical order each time, record `createdAt` fractional digits, distinct-instant count, monotonicity vs write order, and skew; (b) `asyncio.gather` of two `claim_issue`: exactly one GRANTED, the other LOST/CONTENDED naming the winner; (c) A claims with a short lease, wait past expiry, B GRANTED, A renews → `None`, B sole holder on read-back; (d) A acquires {description, marker}; B's intersecting set refused naming A; B's disjoint set granted; (e) release frees for the next holder; (f) a fixture finalizer deletes every marker whose nonce the probe minted, on failure too. Facts go through `tests/probes/recording.record` and are posted here as "[live measurement 2026-09-08]" — public-safe, no configuration values.

**6. Order.** 0 config migration + `docs/migration-v0.2-to-v0.3.md`; 1 this issue (claims, conformance over both implementations); 2 KOD-384/387/388 on the same mechanism (Done on the fake; Evidence gains the live line); 3 probe run + measurement comment; 4 KOD-386/383/385/390 (write gating) stay for the next wave, per the ruling.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-09-08T16:12:30.670Z","updatedAt":"2026-09-08T16:12:30.623Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"f64771e8-b546-47a3-81ac-6a2c40e74831","body":"[v03 audit 2026-09-08]

{"comments":[{"id":"ed90c2c9-475c-445f-8225-ec9d3e599abd","body":"[review synthesis 2026-09-12 · L1 against lane contract] **The port/domain foundation is materially implemented, but L1 cannot close while two founder-owned ownership/approval contracts remain unresolved and one required lease consumer is explicitly absent.**

Current trunk `55a87a5` has the right typed foundation: `ScopeKind` is exactly initiative/project/milestone/issue; `ScopeRef` is vendor-neutral; `scope_issues(ref)` declares container membership vs issue-descendant semantics without bounded-scan fallback; `container_metadata(ref)` preserves milestone semantics; `execution_approved(issue_key)` declares a live self/parent/project/initiative ancestry reread; `writer_identity()` exists for attributable boot checks; and the port documentation keeps deployment claim holder and run-job surface-lease holder as distinct vocabularies. KOD-752 also settles the machine phase-marker vocabulary: `queue:approved:ticket` and `queue:approved:criteria` remain Organize terminal markers resolved through configuration, while `scope:approved` is the human approval fact.

The blocking contracts are now concrete rather than generic:

1. **Approval legibility/ownership is still unruled.** KOD-787 is Todo and explicitly records the shipped failure mode: approval is read in the walker, but an unapproved member is silently dropped, making a wholly unapproved scope observationally equal to an exhausted scope. KOD-751 separately remains Todo on whether the open-decision/Backlog-criterion approval barrier is walker-plan-time only or also an approval-time port refusal. These must be decided together enough that L1/L3 expose one coherent approval contract, not two partial barriers.
2. **Surface leases have no composed holder.** KOD-788 is Todo and records that `acquire_surfaces` / `renew_surfaces` / `release_surfaces` have no `src` call site and `tracker_surface_lease_seconds` has no production consumer. The arbitration primitive itself has been heavily repaired/tested under KOD-747, but KOD-388/KOD-387 cannot close until composition names which component acquires which surface set under the run job id, renews it using configured policy, and releases it.
3. **Issue-state ownership is settled and should be treated as canonical input to the repair, not reopened.** KOD-750's founder ruling chooses the configured run-event→tracker-state table as the *sole* issue-state writer behind the tracker port; the existing lifecycle writer must therefore lose its direct state writes (tracked on KOD-76).

**Heal / acceptance order for L1:** resolve KOD-787 + KOD-751 first (one approval/refusal/legibility policy); resolve KOD-788 by naming the single composed lease consumer and lifecycle; then wire that consumer through the already-repaired ownership primitive and require it at boot. Afterward rerun the L1 conformance criteria specifically for: four scope kinds, subtree/container resolution, live approval ancestry, approval refusal/exclusion observability, disjoint surface ownership, lost/expired lease typed refusal, claim-vs-write-holder separation, configurable duration, writer attribution, and no vendor-specific vocabulary outside the adapter.

Architecture/type verdict: the port and core value objects are strongly typed and hexagonal; the remaining L1 risk is **uncomposed authority**, not a need for more parallel abstractions. Lane fire for the v0.3 scope layer (charter: the v0.3 initiative). Filed 2026-08-07 from the founder charter; consult maturation at the frontier.

**Recorded intent.** The graph's input generalizes from a ticket to a `ScopeRef` — one of `initiative | project | milestone | issue` — accepted at the API/dispatch surface. Resolving a scope means enumerating its issues with relations, states, and container membership through the tracker port.

**Deliverable sketch (matured at consult):**

1. `ScopeRef` as a typed domain value at the API/dispatch surface; an issue-scoped ref resolves to today's single-fire input (the degeneration base case, charter ruling).
2. **Deliberate port widening:** <issue id="188b3e2c-8b7c-430e-8ec6-27d9a6cf3764" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-57/vendor-neutral-tracker-port-linear-adapter-first-of-n-github-issues">KOD-57</issue>'s v0.2 port intentionally excludes container concepts; this lane adds scope containers (initiative/project/milestone) to the port's domain vocabulary — reads only (enumerate issues of a container, container metadata), conformance-suite-tested like every other port capability, each adapter owning its vendor mapping. Recorded as a forward supersession of <issue id="188b3e2c-8b7c-430e-8ec6-27d9a6cf3764" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-57/vendor-neutral-tracker-port-linear-adapter-first-of-n-github-issues">KOD-57</issue>'s exclusion: v0.2's port ships narrow as specced; v0.3 widens it as its own surface.
3. `resolve_scope` as the L0 graph's entry node: `ScopeRef` → the issue set + relation edges the topology planner consumes.
4. **Scope trigger meta-label (founder, 2026-08-07).** The tracker-native way a ScopeRef is registered: a meta label — one level above the untouched granular `queue:` vocabulary — set on an issue (= that issue plus its entire sub-issue subtree; NOTE the deliberate difference from per-issue `queue:approved`, which fires only the issue itself), on a project (= all its milestones and issues), or on an initiative (= everything under it). Label names resolve through OperationConfig's label mapping — never literals in code; the act is recognized from the approver role via state-change provenance, per the <issue id="d180640c-5311-4db5-945c-a3168fb3f951" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-58/approved-fire-auto-dispatch-the-tracker-side-producer-feeding-the-fire">KOD-58</issue> discipline. Two entry points, one resolution: API ScopeRef and tracker meta-label produce the same scope run; the meta-label watcher is the tracker-side producer the scope walker consumes. The two label layers compose: the meta label admits the scope; granular queue labels + blockedBy arithmetic govern what fires inside it.
5. **Approval-label resolution (the hierarchical human act — founder, 2026-08-07; the vocabulary's keystone).** The approval label IS the D4 meta label — **its own top-layer label, NOT a** `queue:` **member, and no extra granular label either: there is deliberately no** `queue:approved:scope` **and no per-issue scope stamp (founder correction, 2026-08-07).** Recorded name `scope:approved` — SETTLED, not open (see A1) — one OperationConfig mapping entry, remappable without code. Set by the APPROVER on any hierarchy node (initiative / project / milestone / issue), it approves implementation of **everything within** that node, and **gates the ENTIRE workflow (stages 1–3): an unapproved scope is never touched by the orchestrator.** The granular queue ladder is extended ONLY by the two machine-set stage markers — `queue:triage` → `queue:proposed` → `queue:approved` (per-issue, standalone, unchanged) — joined by `queue:approved:ticket` / `queue:approved:criteria` inside an approved scope; one OperationConfig `queue_states` mapping (the <issue id="5eee576d-1af6-48ab-ba1f-47587ca52fc2" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-50/adopt-the-scheduled-routine-prompts-fire-prep-grooming-as-the">KOD-50</issue> enum gains the two stage markers; the meta label is its own OperationConfig entry beside it). This lane owns the resolution arithmetic as a port capability: `execution_approved(issue)` iff the issue or any ancestor (parent-issue chain → milestone → project → initiative) carries the meta label with approver provenance — an ancestor walk over container membership, computed never judged at read time, never materialized as a per-issue label, provenance read through the port's state-change surface. The cascade also covers dynamic additions: an issue parented into an approved subtree after approval (e.g. a <issue id="21d33d57-84e2-4e11-a04c-afccc8147969" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-48/shared-remediation-loop-turn-failure-context-into-a-targeted-follow-up">KOD-48</issue> remediation follow-up) resolves approved with no new human act — deliberate. Adapter mapping: Linear natively labels issues, projects, and initiatives; milestone-level carriage is an adapter consult question (candidate: approve at project level, scope the ScopeRef to the milestone).
6. **Write-surface leases — one writer per surface for the duration of a run (F4 of the 2026-08-07 manual scope run).** [KOD-58](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-58/approved-fire-auto-dispatch-the-tracker-side-producer-feeding-the-fire>)'s atomic claim answers *who may FIRE issue X* (its clause 4: "no unexpired claim held through the port's atomic-claim surface"). Nothing answers *who may WRITE surface Y* — while the walker dispatches lanes concurrently ([KOD-75](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-75/v03-l3-topology-planner-scope-walker-blockedby-graph-execution>) D4 configures concurrency and lane caps without stating what makes concurrent writing safe) and every fire, the organize node, the terminal and the audit all write to the tracker. Evidence from the run this lane specs against: each repair pass fixed the surface it owned and falsified a statement on a surface it did not — one told a reader that dependency edges were missing from the graph which the same workflow had recorded minutes earlier — and a hand-maintained do-not-touch list was the only mutex in the system. This is the same deliberate port widening as D2's container reads, conformance-tested the same way.
   * **6a —** `WritableSurface` **as an addressable domain value.** A `StrEnum` of surface kinds plus a frozen value object addressing one surface, in a new module under `src/kodezart/types/domain/` (style precedent: `PersistSource` / `PersistResult`, `types/domain/persist.py:7,20`). Kinds: issue description; marker-keyed comment on an issue; container description; container status update; label set on an issue. A marker-keyed comment surface is addressed by *(issue, marker)* — two components holding different markers on the same issue address different surfaces, and that issue's description is a third, independently held. Neutral references only; no vendor concept in the value, the adapter owns the mapping, exactly as for the container reads.
   * **6b — Exclusive lease per surface, acquired through the port.** The `TrackerPort` protocol ([KOD-57](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-57/vendor-neutral-tracker-port-linear-adapter-first-of-n-github-issues>) D1, `src/kodezart/core/protocols.py`) gains acquire / release / renew over a SET of surfaces for a holder identity — `@runtime_checkable`, mypy-strict, keyword-only, domain vocabulary, in the style of the existing seams (`PRCreator`, `core/protocols.py:282`). Holder identity is the writing run's job id (`generate_job_id`, `src/kodezart/domain/agent.py:6`): a lane fire holds under its own job id, the scope run under the scope run's. Leases govern WRITES only — reads are never leased, so audit and planning arithmetic are unaffected.
   * **6c — Writing a surface you do not hold is a typed error.** A port write to an unheld surface raises a new domain exception in `src/kodezart/domain/errors.py` (beside `WorkspaceError`), carrying the surface and the current holder as primitives — the metadata shape `RateLimitError` uses (`domain/errors.py:16`). Not a warning, not a log line, not last-write-wins. Mechanism: the lease uses the same adapter-owned concurrency primitive as [KOD-57](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-57/vendor-neutral-tracker-port-linear-adapter-first-of-n-github-issues>)'s atomic claim — one primitive, two vocabularies (claim = the right to fire an issue; lease = the right to write a surface) — and under that issue's no-partial-adapters rule a conforming adapter implements both or is not conforming.
   * **6d — Declared surface sets, checked at acquisition.** A writing component declares the surface set it will write and acquires the whole set before its first write. Acquisition is all-or-nothing and never blocks or retries inside the port: on an intersection with a live holder's set it releases whatever it took and raises the typed error naming the intersecting surface and its holder. Contention is therefore discovered at acquisition, never at write time, and two components cannot deadlock each holding half a set. This lane owns the vocabulary, the intersection arithmetic and the enforcement; each writing component names its own declared set in its own lane issue.
   * **6e — Why concurrent lanes are safe, and the one exception.** Lane surface sets are lane-scoped — the lane's own issues, their marker-keyed comments, their labels — so they are disjoint by construction and concurrent lanes never contend. **Question (founder's to rule — label vocabulary is the founder's surface).** The scope-level ladder has THREE functional rungs — a human triages, the machine proposes, a human approves — but only TWO literals exist (`scope:proposed`, machine-set; `scope:approved`, the approver's). What is the third member's **name**, and **who may set it**?

**Why it cannot be left implicit.** Without a computable triage signal the pre-approval grooming mandate has no dispatch predicate: it has nothing to select a scope by, and it collapses back into the shallow heartbeat that the trigger model explicitly distinguishes it from. The rung is functionally present in the ruling of record; only its literal is missing.

**Pinned interim, which this pass proceeds under.** Name `scope:triage`; settable by **any principal** — it expresses prioritization, not authorization, so it is deliberately NOT restricted to the approver role; resolved through OperationConfig by the same ancestor walk as the other two members, and never materialized per issue. The shallow heartbeat is unchanged by this and sets no meta label.

**What flips if the founder rules otherwise.** A different name is one OperationConfig mapping entry and no code. A different *setter* is the material change: restricting it to the approver role makes triage a second human act and changes the grooming mandate's dispatch predicate, so that arm must be ruled before the scope pass is built, not after.

Two questions this lane's meta-label vocabulary leaves open are ruled here, with grounds, so no implementer invents an answer.

**Q9 · Milestone-level label carriage.** RULED: there is **no milestone-level label**. A milestone-scoped run is project-level approval plus a milestone-scoped scope reference — the candidate D5 already names, now settled. *Ground:* it costs zero adapter machinery, and it keeps the port honest for adapters whose backend has no milestone concept at all; a label carried only by some backends would be a capability the conformance suite could not hold every adapter to.

**Q10 · Per-issue exclusion and revocation.** RULED: there is **no exclusion mechanism**. A scope is its subtree; the way to exclude an issue is to not approve it, or to re-parent it out. On revocation, the cascade is re-checked per dispatch (already ruled on the walker lane): in-flight dispatches finish, nothing new dispatches, and nothing is cancelled. Cancellation of in-flight lanes is deferred with its ground recorded on the initiative — machinery with no measured need, over a tick boundary that is already a seam.

*Rider, so the two rulings do not contradict the scope-resolution arithmetic:* "a scope is its subtree" is the ISSUE-ref arm of `ScopeRef`. A container ref — a project, or Q9's milestone-scoped form — resolves by **container membership**, never by walking parent edges. The two arms are different resolutions of one vocabulary, and an implementation that walks parents for a container ref will disagree with the board about what is in scope.

{"comments":[{"id":"c384bf7a-e70e-4dda-a624-18b19b4938c5","body":"[review finding 2026-09-12 · L4 runtime seam] **The run-event table is modeled and validated, but the current composed lifecycle still bypasses it.**

At trunk `55a87a5`, `OperationConfig.run_event_states` is a typed mapping and `require_run_event_table()` enforces the declared `RunEventKind` vocabulary plus DERIVED/NO_TRANSITION constraints. That is good L4 vocabulary work. But `services/tracker_lifecycle.py::TrackerLifecycleWriter` still exposes imperative callbacks (`on_dequeue`, `on_pull_request`, `on_verified_merge`, `on_run_failed`) that directly call `set_workflow_state(stage=...)`, `restore_workflow_state(...)`, and `set_queue_state(...)`. No run event is passed through the configured table at this write seam. PR116 adds run-event stream/alarm port records, but its delta shown so far does not replace this lifecycle transition path with an event-table consumer.

This means the L4 acceptance rule “one total run-event → tracker-state table; exactly one seam applies a row” is not yet the runtime authority: configuration can describe one lifecycle while the writer executes a second hard-coded lifecycle. It also leaves the old verified-merge terminal semantics in a service whose own docstring says merge is the terminal trigger, despite the v0.3 ruling that demonstration in the carrying branch—not later branch fate—is the lane terminal fact.

**Heal:** introduce one typed `apply_run_event(issue_key, event, ...)` port/service seam that resolves the event through `OperationConfig.run_event_states` and is the only route to lifecycle transitions. Existing callbacks should either emit typed events into that seam or disappear. DERIVED/NO_TRANSITION events must provably produce no workflow move. Then delete/forbid direct lifecycle stage selection outside the seam and prove the production composition uses it.

Type-safety verdict: the table itself is strong; the defect is duplicated authority/composition, not weak typing.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-09-12T10:45:30.990Z","updatedAt":"2026-09-12T10:45:30.973Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"fadd7e8b-29c1-447a-8373-09ae74670526","body":"## Architecture review — HIGH: current lifecycle writer directly violates the 2026-09-09 single-state-writer ruling

**Reviewed v0.3 trunk:** `55a87a5`. **Ruling source:** KOD-750 comment `03d4ef8b-cd26-47d7-b2fe-ec5cbef24bcb`.

The founder chose option 1 conditionally and explicitly: the configured run-event → tracker-state table survives and is the **only writer of an issue's workflow state**; the two lifecycle moves become rows in that table; no lifecycle writer writes an issue state; exactly one tracker-port seam applies rows and resolves vendor state names.

Current `services/tracker_lifecycle.py::TrackerLifecycleWriter` still does the opposite:
- `on_dequeue()` calls `tracker.set_workflow_state(... IN_PROGRESS)`;
- `on_pull_request()` calls `set_workflow_state(... IN_REVIEW)`;
- `on_verified_merge()` calls `set_workflow_state(... DONE)` and separately writes queue Done;
- `on_run_failed()` calls `restore_workflow_state(...)` directly.

So the implementation currently has a second state machine beside the ruled transition table, with state choices embedded in lifecycle callbacks. This is precisely the stale/multi-writer design the ruling rejected.

**Smallest correction:** turn `TrackerLifecycleWriter` into an event/effect producer for the parts it still legitimately owns (deliverable ref, gated comments, terminal metadata) and route every workflow-state transition through the one configured transition applier behind the tracker port. Lifecycle callbacks emit/narrow to the corresponding run event; the table determines the effect; the port resolves `LifecycleStage` to vendor state. If a callback has no ruled run-event equivalent yet, that is a missing vocabulary/ruling (e.g. KOD-783/KOD-797), not permission to keep a parallel direct write.

Do not merely wrap these four direct calls in a helper while retaining the hard-coded callback→stage mapping; that preserves the second state machine under another function name.

**Verification:** static/import check leaves exactly one production seam that can apply configured run-event state rows; lifecycle fixtures assert emitted event/effect and resulting tracker state through that seam; adding/changing a transition row in `OperationConfig` changes behavior without editing `TrackerLifecycleWriter`; a fake second tracker passes the same transition conformance without vendor names in services.

**Severity:** High architecture/correctness regression against a founder ruling. **SOLID/DRY/hexagonal:** one source of lifecycle truth, one application seam. **Type safety:** improvement if the event→effect mapping is exhaustive/typed; current direct callbacks make the configured total table non-authoritative.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-09-12T09:16:46.203Z","updatedAt":"2026-09-12T09:16:46.151Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"2e2eb315-a0bb-4bc1-87f6-c2c253fc6049","body":"Architecture/correctness review — **current trunk still writes parent Done from a stale `merged` bit, contradicting the current rollup ruling and L5 delivery semantics.**

Measured at v0.3 trunk `55a87a5`:

- `FireConsolidation.merge_to_feature()` sets `state["merged"] = True` when the ralph/source branch is FAST_FORWARDED or ALREADY_INTEGRATED into the run's **feature branch**. This is internal branch consolidation, not a forge pull-request merge.
- `AuthoredDeliveryCoordinator` then opens a PR, monitors CI, may remediate, and finally emits `AuthoredWorkflowCompleteEvent(... merged=state["merged"], ...)`. The class subclasses `WorkflowCompleteEvent`.
- `LifecycleWatcher._apply()` treats any `WorkflowCompleteEvent` with `event.merged` as a verified merge and calls `TrackerLifecycleWriter.on_verified_merge()`.
- `on_verified_merge()` writes the **parent issue** workflow stage Done and queue state Done.

So a successful inner branch consolidation can make the tracker parent Done at terminal even though L5 explicitly never merges the PR, and even when later delivery/CI terminates unsuccessfully. More fundamentally, KOD-755's current ruling says a parent's Done is a subtree rollup/read and **no step writes a parent's Done**.

This is a semantic collision caused by overloading `merged` for two meanings across layers. The smallest repair is to remove this lifecycle parent-Done transition from the watcher/writer under the current ruling. Criterion/lane-check sub-issue state is the authoritative live state; the parent Done is derived by rollup. If an external-delivery terminal fact still needs recording, give it a distinct delivery outcome/type rather than reusing the fire graph's internal-consolidation `merged` flag.

Verification should include: (1) inner consolidation succeeds + CI red -> parent is not written Done; (2) inner consolidation succeeds + PR open/green -> no parent Done write occurs, rollup answers from sub-issues; (3) no `on_verified_merge`/equivalent parent setter remains reachable under the KOD-755 ruling.
