Lane fire for the v0.3 scope layer (charter: the v0.3 initiative). Filed 2026-08-07 from the founder charter; consult maturation at the frontier.

**Recorded intent.** The tracker stops being documentation about runs and becomes the **live state store of runs**. During a scope run: the evaluator's per-criterion verdicts feed the criterion axis, and an issue's state follows from D9's arithmetic over **both** axes — never from the accept verdict directly, and never from a landing event (Rulings A and B) — with the owning branch recorded (the issue↔branch association from dispatch); criteria validation (<issue id="0f2121ea-dc02-45c6-895a-3f9ed503f1f9" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-66/kodezart-generate-criteria-infeasible-or-mutually-unsatisfiable">KOD-66</issue>'s gate) reads the issue's spec from the tracker as the source; the per-lane lifecycle writes generalize <issue id="d180640c-5311-4db5-945c-a3168fb3f951" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-58/approved-fire-auto-dispatch-the-tracker-side-producer-feeding-the-fire">KOD-58</issue>'s single-fire write-back to every lane of the scope.

**Deliverable sketch (matured at consult):**

 1. Evaluator write-back: per-criterion cross-offs are written through the tracker port **as the evaluator produces them, inside the loop and at evaluator cadence** — the site and cadence are [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D8 — each carrying the verification evidence (test names, event payloads) the protocol's evidence rule requires. **This deliverable writes no issue state.** State follows from D9's arithmetic over both axes and is applied through D6a's table: computed, never a model-judged transition. Deliverable 7e records why the accept verdict alone cannot carry it, and Ruling A why no landing event may. An earlier revision read "accepted iteration → issue Done"; that is corrected here at source rather than superseded in place.
 2. Validation from the tracker: <issue id="0f2121ea-dc02-45c6-895a-3f9ed503f1f9" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-66/kodezart-generate-criteria-infeasible-or-mutually-unsatisfiable">KOD-66</issue>'s validator and the criteria pipeline read the issue spec (the organize node's output) as ground truth; the persisted criteria artifact (<issue id="77fdb019-dbd0-466b-8632-fdfa44d848f5" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-11/criteria-mutate-between-persisted-kodezartcriteriajson-and-evaluator">KOD-11</issue>'s byte-stable, id-keyed shape) records its tracker provenance.
 3. Deviation discipline mechanized: a fire that must deviate from spec records the deviation on the issue **before** the deviating code lands — tracker first, then code (the standing rule, now enforced by the machinery). Order alone is not legitimacy: who rules on the deviation, on what grounds, and what happens when the claim is refused is the criterion amendment reconciler (<issue id="24fe88e8-9fa6-4f4c-90e6-df8cd138439f" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-97/criterion-amendment-reconciler-default-upheld-amend-only-on-a-self">KOD-97</issue>), which owns that contract in full.
 4. **Remote as the durable substrate ("work on remote" — charter ruling 2026-08-07).** Branch state is pushed as work proceeds, so partial results survive process death: the work itself, and the id-keyed criteria artifact on the branch, are always recoverable from remote. Combined with the tracker state, this makes "what is still missing" a computable set across any death — no in-process state is ever load-bearing for resume. What the tracker actually carries about a lane while that work is still in flight — the record's content, its cadence, its writer, the edit-vs-post notification split, and its role as the re-entry index — is <issue id="fd0a7f05-6186-4668-8898-d10214693efc" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and">KOD-96</issue>.
 5. **Evaluator as reconciler.** On a resumed branch, the loop's first evaluate pass grades the existing branch state per criterion id; already-satisfied criteria pass without any new execution, and only the failing set drives work. Resume burns tokens on the delta only — the loop begins with what is still missing, never with what already sits remote.
 6. **Run-event → tracker-state table (added 2026-08-07 from the reference run).** Deliverable 1 rules the transition computed rather than judged, but gave the writer nothing to compute against: the lifecycle writes existed as event→state pairs in a prose parenthetical, and <issue id="d180640c-5311-4db5-945c-a3168fb3f951" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-58/approved-fire-auto-dispatch-the-tracker-side-producer-feeding-the-fire">KOD-58</issue>'s `workflow_states` is a **name** mapping (semantic member → tracker identifier), not an event mapping. With only those two the writer still chooses — and in the reference run it chose wrong in both directions: an issue sat In Progress for eighteen days with zero implementation, and the landing step wrote issues In Progress while their PRs were open, understating the run's own progress.

    a. **A declared run-event → tracker-state table in** `OperationConfig`**, beside** `workflow_states` **and not replacing it.** **The table's key set is the run-event vocabulary, which [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D4 owns and declares.** This table is keyed on exactly that set and carries no roster of its own, so adding an event to the vocabulary and adding its row here are one revision rather than two. Each value is a semantic state member, an explicit `NO_TRANSITION`, or D9c's `DERIVED`. The value assignments this deliverable rules:
    * `DERIVED` — D9c's set: `evaluator accepted`, `audit refuted`, `criterion refuted`, `landed and verified`. Under the arithmetic none of them may name a state directly.
    * `NO_TRANSITION` — `first push`, which the live record carries ([KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D2); `gate green` and `gate red`, which are loop state rather than lane state and which the record likewise carries; `escalation raised`, whose carriers are its posted comment and the `decision` label ([KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D11a, D11c) — a question being open says nothing about how far the lane has got; and `issue crossed off`, which is the **result** of a `DERIVED` recomputation and must never be the event that writes that state a second time.
    * **A named state member** — `lane dispatched`, `PR opened`, `checks green`, `lane plateaued` (<issue id="bb89b7b1-71e9-49d9-bb71-e65a6bb64742" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-40/ralph-loop-stop-when-progress-stalls-and-open-a-do-not-merge-pr-from">KOD-40</issue>), `criteria halt` (<issue id="0f2121ea-dc02-45c6-895a-3f9ed503f1f9" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-66/kodezart-generate-criteria-infeasible-or-mutually-unsatisfiable">KOD-66</issue>), `claim lost` (<issue id="d180640c-5311-4db5-945c-a3168fb3f951" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-58/approved-fire-auto-dispatch-the-tracker-side-producer-feeding-the-fire">KOD-58</issue>).

    A vocabulary member with no row here is D6b's typed boot error, which is why these assignments are stated rather than left to a writer to supply: as the two bodies stood, **five** events declared posted carried no row — `gate green`, `gate red`, `issue crossed off`, `criterion refuted` and `escalation raised` — so every run halted at startup by construction. Neither body was wrong on its own.

    b. **The writer applies the table and never chooses.** Total lookup, no default arm — <issue id="a4fdc34e-d183-40cf-b77a-16f1459c6c72" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-30/workflow-complete-has-no-outcome-discriminator-review-failure-exit">KOD-30</issue>'s rule applied to the state writer. A run event with no row is a typed **boot** error, never a runtime guess.

    c. **Precedence.** The table is applied to the lane's LATEST event. A transition that moves a lane backwards (In Review → In Progress) requires an explicit row permitting it; absent that row it is a typed error. This is what makes the run's concrete failure — In Progress written over an open PR — unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged.

    d. **Drift reconciliation on each walker tick.** A lane's tracker state is recomputed from its live run state (<issue id="fd0a7f05-6186-4668-8898-d10214693efc" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and">KOD-96</issue>'s record) and corrected when the two disagree. That is what catches the stale-In-Progress failure, without waiting for the L7 audit to find it.
 7. **Two axes, gated independently (E3 and E4 of the [edge-case catalogue](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and#comment-c17fd466-5e12-499e-9962-cbadcff0a2cc>) on [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>), which stays the cross-lane index — the cases owned by other lanes are read there, not restated here).** Deliverable 1 crosses an issue off on "the accept verdict", which is a verdict on ONE property. The 2026-08-08 audit of the reference run's first lane returned refutations that were almost entirely departures from rulings pinned hours earlier rather than criterion failures; collapsed onto a single axis, a lane that satisfied nearly all of its criteria read as satisfying none, and the response was to cross off nothing. Criterion satisfaction and pinned-ruling compliance are independent properties of a branch, and are recorded, rendered and gated as such.

    a. **The compliance axis needs a record; the criterion axis already has one.** The criterion axis is `CriterionCrossOff`, **defined in full by** [KOD-96 ](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>)**D8b** — its name, its fields and its `CrossOffState` are read there and are not restated here, and there is **never a second per-criterion model**. New module `src/kodezart/types/domain/lane_gate.py` — one typed partition per module, the `types/domain/consolidation.py` precedent — carries only what the gate adds: frozen `CamelCaseModel`s `RulingMark(ruling_id: RulingId, state: CrossOffState, graded_sha: str, violating_sha: str | None, evidence: str)` — **the state enum and not a boolean**, for the reason [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D10e gives for every record carrying a graded sha: a mark graded at a sha the head has moved past is not compliant and not violating, it is ungraded, and a boolean has no word for that; `LaneCheck` (D8a); and `LaneGate(cross_offs: tuple[CriterionCrossOff, ...], rulings: tuple[RulingMark, ...], lane_checks: tuple[LaneCheck, ...])`. `RulingId` is the per-ruling identity type minted by the fire-time ruling node at the single site [KOD-94](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-94/fire-time-ruling-node-rule-every-open-question-onto-the-tracker-before>) D9 establishes, retrieved as a checkable list through [KOD-97](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-97/criterion-amendment-reconciler-default-upheld-amend-only-on-a-self>) D8; like `criterion_id` it is referenced and never a copy of the text it addresses.

    b. **The ruling axis is graded by the same reader that grades criteria, at the same sha.** Each evaluation pass produces a `CriterionCrossOff` set and a `RulingMark` set together, so no writer is the last thing to touch the branch before a cross-off. The inputs already exist at `main` @ `92597c0` and are thrown away: `_evaluate_node` receives per-criterion results and the sha they were graded at in one place and emits both on `WorkflowIterationEvent` (`src/kodezart/chains/ralph_loop.py:238-250`; the event at `src/kodezart/types/domain/agent.py:347-355`), then reduces them to `accepted = all(r.passed …)` and `pending_failures` (`ralph_loop.py:238`, `:252-255`) — a passing criterion leaves no per-criterion record anywhere, and nothing records the ruling axis at all.

    c. **E4 — a criterion satisfied BY forbidden code is named, never ticked away.** `laundered(cross_off, marks, commits)`, a pure function in D9's module, is true when some `RulingMark` at `FAILING` has a `violating_sha` standing at or before that cross-off's `graded_sha` in the lane's recorded commit order (`LaneRunState.commits`, [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D1) — the criterion was graded over code carrying the violation, so its passing state may rest on it. Arithmetic over data the record already holds: no new git read, and no new field on the cross-off. A laundered cross-off stays visible as passing on the criterion axis **and** blocks on the ruling axis; D9's arithmetic refuses Done on it. This is what lets the machine say "every criterion satisfied, still not shippable" instead of having to pick one of those two sentences and suppress the other.

    d. **Both axes are separately visible, and neither is rendered as the other's summary.** How a criterion's state is recorded — and, load-bearingly, **for which shapes a body write happens at all** — is [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D9's: the checkbox shape is flipped in place, and the other three carry their state on the record alone, because writing to those lines is the restructuring E1 forbids. **This deliverable mandates no line edit of its own, for any shape** — an earlier revision read as requiring one for every shape, which contradicted that ruling. The address those writes resolve against is <issue id="66332a93-910c-4529-bda6-f530a3c45f24" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-95/idempotent-tracker-writes-marker-keyed-comments-assert-then-edit">KOD-95</issue> D8. What this deliverable adds is the second surface: the ruling axis is its own marker-keyed comment, **edited in place and therefore silent**, under [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D4's edit-vs-post split.

    e. **Amends deliverable 1 and the recorded intent.** The accept verdict feeds the criterion axis and nothing else; no tracker state follows from it directly. State follows from D9's arithmetic over both axes.
 8. **Lane-level checks have their own tick site (E2).** A fire's own Verification checks are properties of the lane, not of any sub-issue — the reference run's first lane carried numbered lane checks and no sub-issue owned any of them. A model in which only sub-issues carry criteria makes a fire's Done a pure function of its children, which is wrong: a lane can have every child Done and still fail its own integration checks.

    a. `LaneCheck(check_id: str, state: CrossOffState, graded_sha: str, capability_required: EnvironmentCapability | None, evidence: str)` in D7a's module — the state enum and not a boolean, for D7a's reason; and the requirement field because a fire's own integration check can need a resource as readily as a criterion's demonstration can. That field is the only route to the state it unlocks and D7a's `RulingMark` deliberately carries none, which is what makes that state unreachable for a mark by construction; the rule and the vocabulary are [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) 10j's and are not restated here. Addressed against the **fire issue's own** Verification section through <issue id="66332a93-910c-4529-bda6-f530a3c45f24" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-95/idempotent-tracker-writes-marker-keyed-comments-assert-then-edit">KOD-95</issue> D8, which resolves its shape — a second write site beside the sub-issue cross-offs, not a re-use of one of them. **Where the write goes follows the shape, and this deliverable does not override it:** a fire's Verification checks are numbered rather than checkboxes, which is the `VERIFICATION_CHECK` shape [KOD-96](<https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-96/live-lane-run-state-record-marker-keyed-edited-at-commit-cadence-and>) D9b writes no body for, so the state lives on the lane-gate record through <issue id="66332a93-910c-4529-bda6-f530a3c45f24" href="https://linear.app/duckburg/issue/KOD-95/idempotent-tracker-writes-marker-keyed-comments-assert-then-edit">KOD-95</issue> D1's marker-keyed comment. D2's assert-then-edit is used only for a fire that carries its checks as checkboxes. An earlier revision routed every lane-check write through D2 unconditionally, which would have inserted checkboxes into the exact bodies E1 forbids restructuring.

    b. A fire's Done is `all sub-issues Done AND all lane checks satisfied` — **two sets** — where *satisfied* means for a lane check exactly what D9a says it means for a criterion, read off the same enum. ## Groomed amendment — v0.3 roadmap application (2026-08-11)

**Anchor ruling (baseline).** Code references in this body are anchored at a superseded baseline. The base is the v0.2 union integration branch. A line reference is a pointer, never a spec claim; re-derive it against the base before opening the file, and a reference that no longer resolves is a stale pointer, not a defect in the deliverable.

**M4-1 — the criteria write-back model (founder ruling, 2026-08-11): the checklist lives on the issue body, the tick is silent, and one separate step alone sets Done.** Three consequences bind this lane, and they replace the marker-comment carriage for criterion satisfaction:

* **Carriage.** The Linear adapter's carriage of criterion satisfaction is the **body checklist itself**, written by stage 2 into the issue body. Per-criterion marker-comment streams are retired. The **port vocabulary is unchanged** — satisfaction stays identity-addressed and graded-sha-stamped — so this is an adapter carriage change, not a model change.
* **Tick mechanics.** During the loop the evaluator ticks each demonstrated criterion **in place, at evaluator cadence, with the sha it was graded at inline**, as a **silent edit**. D9a's rendering rules follow the shape as before; what changes is that the checkbox now carries the graded sha rather than state alone, and that it IS read back.
* **The Done-setter split (D9a gains it).** The per-criterion tick **never moves a state**. A **separate big-picture evaluation step**, running in fresh context and independent of the ticking loop, **alone** sets an issue's and a fire's state to Done. `resolve_issue_state` and `resolve_fire_state` are unchanged as arithmetic; what is ruled is **who is allowed to apply their result**. The standing independent audit is unchanged and is NOT substituted by this step — two readers, two cadences, neither discharging the other.
* *Design ground, recorded because it generalizes:* **minimal comment volume.** Comments are for lane events, escalations and evidence a human must be notified of. A durable fact that evolves belongs in an in-place edit on its one surface.

**M4-2 — the forge arm of Done arithmetic (folds into D1/D9).** Carried verbatim from the roadmap so no wording is invented at build time:

> **Forge arm of Done arithmetic.** Beside the local gate and the criterion checklist, Done takes the forge run at the graded sha as an input, with three arms. (1) *Run-exists:* a forge run exists for a graded sha iff at least one check run reports a head sha equal to that sha exactly — ref-name match, latest-on-branch, and ancestor shas do not count. No such run is the no-run arm: never green, never red; close-out blocks until a run exists at that sha or the scope's operation configuration declares the ref forge-exempt (a declared state, never inferred). (2) *Which checks count:* the counted check-name roster is operation configuration resolved per scope, never a literal in the node; `CheckStep` supplies each name's gate-vs-cascade role. Filed by the stage-2 validator for that milestone: an independent grader, fresh context, running at the writer tier under the recorded tier deviation. 73 criteria across 5 issues were swept against the v0.2 union integration branch at `55b5525`. Every finding below is a gap in the shipped criteria contract itself, not in the criteria that exposed it. Each names what it was measured on.

**1. No verdict exists for a model-lease conflict.** A criterion can oblige a lane to add a field to a model another lane declares under a model lease. The sweep grades demonstrability, the field is demonstrable, so the verdict is `feasible` and the conflict is invisible at the criteria stage. Neither the two-armed fault line nor the forbidden-class set names ownership. *Measured on:* the landedness-carrier criterion of the squashed-blocker issue, which adds a three-state field to a model this lane's model owns. *Consequence:* a lease violation is discovered by an implementer, at the point where the only remaining options are to violate it or to stop.

**2. The forbidden-class screen is prose, and 5 of 5 issues reproduced the same violation.** Every member of the milestone minted a criterion of the form "`make check` green" — precisely the `execution_graded` class the drafter's own instruction bans. Five out of five is not a drafter lapse; it is the absence of a mechanical check on the write path. *What the stage-2 node needs:* a deterministic screen at the moment the checklist is written, not an instruction to a model plus an adversarial reader downstream. The repair is already known and stated in the same contract — the negative-shape proxy over suppressions and weakened test surface — so it can be applied mechanically rather than judged.

**3. The write surface has no write-back read, and the tracker transforms markup on write.** The checklist now lives in the issue body, which is a durable surface. Observed this pass: a parenthetical note appended to one criterion had its italic and code fences re-flowed by the tracker on write. **Criterion ids survived only because every one of them is fenced as code** — bare identifiers elsewhere in the same bodies were rewritten into link elements. Ids are the keys verdicts, ruling marks and audit findings hang on, so an id mangled on write breaks all three silently. *What the contract must state:* id fencing is a requirement of the write, and the writer reads the stored line back and compares before it claims the write.

**4. `vacuous_at_base` has a consequence in code and none on the durable surface.** The sweep forces a soft downgrade on a flagged criterion, but that consequence lives in the validation output; the checklist line carries no flag. *Measured:* five criteria of the walker lane's fire are already satisfied at the base, before any work exists. A later grader reading the body alone cannot distinguish a criterion that discriminates from one satisfied by the empty implementation. The flag belongs in the shape of the checklist line.

**5. The fault line has no arm for "the deliverable is superseded by the base" — and this is the expensive one.** The repair set has exactly two members: an edit to the criterion's text, or something supplied to the environment. A criterion faithfully EXTRACTED from a body whose mechanism the base has already replaced is at fault in neither: the extraction is correct and no resource helps. It currently classifies as `criterion_text` infeasible, which routes it back to the drafter for a repair the drafter cannot make, spends the one regeneration round, and halts. *Measured:* five criteria of the plan-time base-resolvability issue plus one on the walker lane's fire, all resting on a base-resolution rule the base replaced with an incompatible one. **The missing arm routes to the TICKET stage, not to the drafter** — a body-level supersession is not a criterion edit.

**6. One regeneration round is measured too small on the extract path, and only there.** For generated criteria one round is defensible. For extracted criteria an infeasible verdict usually indicts the body rather than the criterion, so the round is spent on a repair that cannot succeed and the halt is reached having learned nothing the first pass did not already know. Pair this with finding 5's routing: the extract path needs its own budget and its own destination.

**7. The hard/soft classification is generated and never validated.** The sweep flags pinned literals but never checks that a criterion measuring a SHAPE was classified soft. All 73 criteria in this milestone were authored hard, including static import assertions, enum-value pins and naming-convention checks. Since the class decides what a failure costs downstream, an unvalidated classification is a cost model nobody checked.

Stage 2 of the v0.3 workflow needs exactly that: it validates criteria EXTRACTED from a tracker body, in a run where nothing generated them. The battle test substituted a dispatched judge session implementing the same contract by hand. The stage-2 node cannot ship without the standalone surface.

**2. `literal_count` silently disarms this board's central DRY guard.** The contract flags a literal count of internal symbols as an observation rather than a fault — correct — and the harness draws the consequence of forcing the criterion to `soft_signal`, out of the hard-gate partition. But the v0.3 board expresses its single-writer and single-definition-site invariants *precisely as* exactly-one-call-site static checks. Measured in M2: five criteria across three issues are marked `(hard)` by their author and would be downgraded by the harness — the gap-computation single site, the mandate-kind single dispatch site, the no-label-literal check, the change-timestamp non-read check, and the consumed-list single-definition check. So the criteria carrying the architecture's most load-bearing guarantees would become non-blocking, and nothing on the board says so. Either the class needs a carve-out for architectural single-site assertions, or the board needs to stop expressing invariants that way — this lane owns which.

**3. `execution_graded` has no scope qualifier, and it bit every issue in the milestone.** All four sets carried a "`make check` is green" criterion; all four are `infeasible` under the contract, because a command whose execution grades it is unreachable to an evaluator collecting evidence by reading the changeset. Repaired to the negative-shape proxy. But the class is stated absolutely while the run's own house rules require a grader to run the gate and to check the forge run at the graded sha — so the same run both forbids and mandates execution-grading, at different grains. The contract needs to say which grader it binds. Until it does, every extracted criteria set will carry this defect, because "the gate is green" is how humans write acceptance criteria.

**4. Nothing in the contract screens for a criterion admitting two readings.** One M2 criterion did (whole-file vs added-text scope), and the whole-file reading was refuted at base while the added-text reading was satisfiable — so the same criterion is both `infeasible` and `feasible` depending on the reader. The organize lane's admission test already names "a criterion admitting two readings" as a refusal class at the TICKET stage; the criteria contract has no counterpart at the CRITERIA stage, and the two stages grade different objects. Ambiguity reached the validator and was caught only because it was looked for.

**5. Conjunction satisfiability found a real contradiction the per-criterion pass could not.** In M2 one set was jointly unsatisfiable at minimal subset {byte-identity over nine sections, no-section-contradicts-another}: two of the nine sections carry cross-references to sections the target file does not have, so transcribing them byte-identically installs dangling references. Both criteria are individually `feasible`. This is evidence the conjunction pass is load-bearing rather than ceremonial, and it must survive into the shipped stage-2 node rather than being treated as a best-effort in-prompt self-check.

**6. The write surface rewrites the markup a validator writes into it.** A stage-2 note written into a checklist line with nested emphasis around inline-code identifiers came back with the emphasis run collapsed and broken mid-sentence. The identifiers survived only because they were backticked. Two consequences for this lane's addressing scheme: criterion ids must be stored in inline code, and that is a mechanism rather than a style choice; and any in-line annotation the loop writes must be markup-minimal, because the surface normalizes on write and the writer never sees it.

Each was hit while grading, not imagined.

**1 — The repair set has two members and a scope run needs a third: a criterion blocked by a SIBLING LANE.** The contract's environment arm names a service, runtime, credential, fixture or network. A criterion blocked because the type it consumes is another lane's unlanded deliverable is none of those, and the text arm is plainly wrong — the criterion's text is correct and editing it would be the mistake. Two criteria on the scope terminal are exactly this, and they were stamped `unverifiable` with the blocker named because that is the closest admissible reading, not because it fits. In a single-fire loop this case did not exist; a scope walk creates it structurally, since lanes are dispatched from one graph and each other's artifacts are the normal input. Either the environment arm is widened with a ruling that says so, or a fourth arm is minted — but a validator left to improvise this will improvise it differently every time.

**2 — Every observation the contract collects has nowhere to land on the durable surface.** The shipped finding carries pinned literals, a base demonstration with the command it ran, a cost claim with its measurement, a forbidden class, and undeclared switch arms — none of which is a repair, all of which the harness draws consequences from. A body checklist line has a tick box and a sentence. So a grader either drops them (losing what the contract deliberately collects) or inflates the criterion text with grading residue (making the criterion less readable at every future tick). This pass parked them in a per-issue comment, which no machine reads. The stage-2 node needs a per-criterion observation carrier that is not the criterion's text.

**3 — The base-naming rule fires on criteria that carry their base one line above them.** The drafter contract requires any scope or no-touch criterion to name its base IN THE CRITERION'S OWN TEXT, on the ground that a bare base lets the grader pick trunk and convict a stacked lane of every edit it inherited. Sound — and it assumes criteria travel as a bare list. On the body-checklist surface they travel under a provenance line that names the base explicitly, so a strict reading makes every base-relative criterion in this milestone infeasible on a technicality. Four were repaired that way this pass. The rule should either admit a set-level base declaration when the criteria are stored with one, or say plainly that it does not — the current text forces a regeneration round to buy nothing.

**Adjacent, smaller, and worth one line: the tracker transforms text on write.** Square brackets in an appended blocker stamp came back escaped. Content survived; ids in code spans survived intact across all four members. Five gaps in the shipped criteria contract, each hit while validating 142 criteria across this model's eight members. Filed on this lane because it is the criterion-lifecycle fire; each names the capability the stage-2 node needs rather than a wording preference.

**CG-1 — the contract cannot tell "graded by reading the named test" from "graded by running a command", and the difference decides 142 verdicts.** The forbidden-class list names `execution_graded` — *a command whose EXECUTION is what grades it*. Nearly every criterion on this model is phrased as the outcome of a named fixture ("a fixture whose … fails", "running the node twice leaves …"). Read literally, all of them are execution-graded and the whole milestone returns infeasible. Read as the drafter's own instruction intends — falsifiable from evidence the in-loop evaluator collects by reading the changeset — "the named test exists on the graded branch and asserts exactly this" is readable evidence, and they are all fine. **Both readings are available and the contract states neither.** A judge that picks the first destroys a correct board; one that picks the second is exercising undocumented discretion. This pass took the second and recorded it, which is precisely the heuristic-standing-in-for-judgment the evaluation is supposed to catch. **Needed: the discrimination stated in the contract itself.** This is the highest-value gap of the five — it decides every verdict on this board and is currently settled by whoever grades.

**CG-2 — `unverifiable` has a verdict but no carriage on the durable surface.** The refuter emits a `missing_resource` per criterion; the checklist line is the durable surface criteria evolve on; the tick's line format is pinned to a state-and-sha pair. **No slot is declared for a blocker stamp.** One criterion in this milestone is genuinely unverifiable, and recording it meant inventing a free-text convention on the line — a second writer of the same line would not know the format. Needed: the blocker stamp pinned like the tick is, or a declared place off the line.

**CG-3 — a repair that requires a SIBLING member's vocabulary widening has no propagation mechanism.** Observed here rather than reasoned: five criteria on the demonstration-evidence member named a verdict and a field the declaring member does not declare. The bounded regeneration round is scoped **per issue**; the correct fix necessarily involves two — the criterion, and the member that declares the vocabulary. A per-issue judge is left with two bad options: mass-fail the set, or silently enlarge a second member's scope. The repair taken was to state the criterion as *the type gains the case, naming the type*, which the drafter's own rule prescribes — but nothing carries the consequence to the declaring member's verbatim-members criterion except a human writing it down. Needed: the contract to say what happens when the smallest repair crosses an issue boundary.

**CG-4 — conjunction satisfiability is scoped per issue, so cross-member conflicts inside one model are invisible to it.** The contract asks whether one implementation satisfies every criterion **in this set**. This model is built in one pass under one write lease, so the real question is whether one implementation satisfies every criterion across all eight members. One candidate conflict surfaced across two members and resolved only under a pinned reading; it was found by holding all eight sets at once, which no per-issue judge does. **This is the same defect class the model-agreement member exists to catch one level up, and the criteria contract has no equivalent.** Needed: a set-level conjunction pass over a model's members, or an explicit statement that cross-member conflicts are out of scope and owned elsewhere.

**CG-5 — the base-naming rule is unenforceable on board-resident criteria.** The contract requires a scope criterion to name its base in the criterion's own text. On this board the base is pinned in the fire body's stage-1 rulings and no criterion text carries one; nothing checks the two agree. Not triggered in this milestone — no scope or no-touch criterion is present, verified — but the mechanism is absent and the next milestone that writes one will find out at grading time.

Filed from the stage-2 validation of the delivery-and-terminate milestone, 2026-08-12. The battle-test brief asks the run to attempt ONCE, seriously, to drive the composed tree's real criteria validator standalone over board criteria. It was attempted. It fails, and it fails at the type boundary rather than at the model.

**The measurement.** The composed tree derives its criterion-id pattern from a single prefix constant and pins it as `^AC-[1-9][0-9]*$`. Three types enforce it at construction: the generated-criterion model's `id`, the refuter finding's `criterion_id`, and the list-element alias used wherever ids travel inside a list. The board's stage-2 ids are issue-qualified — `KOD-77-AC-1`, `KOD-110-AC-10` — and none matches. Checked directly: the fire-local form matches, every issue-qualified form does not.

**Why this is a contract gap and not an id-format preference.** The fourth decision of 2026-08-11 put the criteria checklist on the ISSUE BODY, which makes a criterion id a name in a scope-wide namespace: several issues in one scope each carry their own criteria, an evaluator ticks them in place across issues, and the run supervisor and audit both refer to them across lanes. A fire-local `AC-n` is ambiguous the moment two issues in one scope both have an `AC-3`. The minting scheme and the durable surface were decided by different acts and disagree.

**Consequence for the stage-2 node.** As shipped it cannot ingest board criteria at all — not degraded, not partial: every finding and every criterion raises at model construction, so the sweep, the grounding of stated verdicts against their evidence, the conjunction reconciliation and the regeneration-target computation are all unreachable over this input. The pure classification and reconciliation functions are otherwise reusable as-is; the pattern is the whole blocker.

**What this milestone's validation had to substitute, so the manual step is visible rather than invisible.** Three-state verdicts, smallest-repair fault lines, measured-cost discipline, forbidden-class screening and conjunction satisfiability were all applied by judgment against the shipped contract's own text, with the verdicts recorded as per-issue comments. Nothing machine-checked the verdict against its evidence the way the shipped grounding validator would have, which is exactly the check the manual substitution loses.

**The repair belongs here, not in the prompt.** Either the pattern admits an issue-qualified form and the minting function produces one, or the id stays fire-local and the body-checklist surface carries the qualification separately — one of the two, decided once, because the id is what the tick, the audit trace and the cross-lane reference all key on.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-08-12T06:09:11.598Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-12T06:09:11.563Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"f1222244-7b33-478e-aaa5-00096c440cd0","body":"[finding] 2026-08-12 · stage-2 criteria validation, M6 (KOD-79) — six contract gaps the criterion-lifecycle lane has to close

Filed from the v0.3 stage-1/2 battle test. Each item is something the stage-2 node needs and the shipped contract does not give it. Evidence re-derived at the composed base `origin/kodezart/integration-v02-full` @ `55b5525`; provisional pending top-tier re-verification (tier deviation recorded for this act).

**G1 — minted criterion ids are not issue-qualified, so they cannot be board-durable.** `mint_criteria` in `domain/criteria.py` assigns `AC-n` in emission order — its own docstring says so. A checklist living on an issue body needs `KOD-n-AC-m`, because bare `AC-3` collides across every issue in a scope and resolves to nothing once a comment, a report or a run-state record cites it out of context. Stage 2 qualified all 24 ids by hand. Either minting takes the issue key, or the write surface does — but one of them must, and today neither does.

**G2 — the tracker rewrites bare issue keys on write, and only an unwritten convention protects criterion ids from it.** Writing `KOD-74` into a body returns it as an issue reference, not as the text that was sent; this write produced 21 such transformations in one section. Criterion ids survived only because the author fenced every one in backticks. That convention appears in no contract, no prompt and no type — a future writer that emits `KOD-79-AC-9` unfenced has its id silently transformed and every downstream tick keyed on it stops resolving. A criterion id is an identity and must round-trip verbatim through the port; the port should assert the round-trip rather than the author remembering a formatting trick. **Second face of the same gap:** the transformation injects workspace URLs into a body that mirrors to a public repository, which the public-board rule forbids and which no writer put there.

**G3 — `unverifiable`-pending-blocker has no durable representation.** The shipped validator emits `unverifiable` with a `missing_resource`, and that verdict is admissible — but the checklist line format is `- [ ] <id> *(class)* — <text>`, which has no field for it. The blocker had to be stamped inline as prose. Consequence: no later reader can compute "which criteria in this scope are gated on which unlanded lane" — the exact query a walker needs before it dispatches. The verdict is machine-made and then flattened to prose at the only surface that persists.

**G4 — a scope criterion must name its base, but the base is not known when the checklist is written.** The drafter contract requires any scope, no-touch or modifies-only criterion to state `{{base_ref}}` in its own text, and rightly: a bare diff base convicts a stacked lane of every edit it inherited. But `{{base_ref}}` resolves at fire time, while stage 2 writes the checklist durably in advance — so the author must hard-code a literal (here, the composed integration branch). If the walker later fires the lane stacked on its blocker's branch, that literal is wrong and the criterion mis-grades in exactly the direction the rule exists to prevent. A durable checklist needs a deferred base reference the loop resolves, not a literal frozen at authoring time.

**G5 — nothing checks a criterion's named cross-lane symbol against the fire's blocker closure.** Three of KOD-79's criteria name a symbol owned by another lane that no edge orders before this fire; the criteria are correct and the graph is what is missing. Stage 2 caught it only because a human-shaped grade walked the blocker edges by hand. The check is cheap and mechanical: for every symbol a criterion names as imported-from-another-lane, the owning issue must be in this issue's transitive `blockedBy` closure, or the criterion is `unverifiable` with that issue as its blocker. Without it, stage 2 can certify a set that no implementation can demonstrate at dispatch, and the walker learns this only after spending a fire.

**G6 — the composed validator cannot be driven over board criteria without three substitutions.** The battle test built a standalone harness around the real machinery — the shipped refuter prompt and its registry, criterion minting, ticket rendering, the structured-output schema, the live dispatch, the sweep and its regeneration-target arithmetic, all imported rather than reimplemented. It ran. What it had to substitute is precisely the stage-2 node's missing surface: the board-issue-to-ticket-draft mapping, the Verification-section-to-drafted-criterion extraction, and the graph-only execution surfaces. Those three substitutions ARE the node — everything else already exists and works. A fourth gap showed in its output: the harness's findings came back keyed `AC-1`, `AC-2`, …, which is G1 observed end-to-end rather than argued.

Surfaced by taking the battle test's stated preference seriously: the composed tree's REAL criteria-feasibility sweep was driven standalone over a board criteria set — the 26 criteria a stage-2 author wrote into the M1 lane fire's body per the fourth [decision] of 2026-08-11. It ran, twice (pre- and post-repair), and produced the verdicts, the minimal conflicting subset and the regeneration targets that pass recorded. These are the places where it does not reach the board.

**1. The criterion identity type cannot express an issue-qualified id.** The shipped identity pattern admits `AC-<n>` and nothing else, and the list-element alias re-checks the same pattern, so `KOD-73-AC-1` is rejected at model construction. Driving the sweep required mapping every board id down to its bare form and back by hand. Stage 2 mints issue-qualified ids because criteria now live on many issues at once inside one scope run; the type still assumes one criteria set per run, where positional uniqueness was enough. Whoever owns the id scheme widens the pattern, or the loop cannot address in types the criterion it has just written to a body.

**2. Regeneration targets sweep in the innocent member of a conflict.** Every id named by a retained contradiction joins the regeneration targets, and the drafter is instructed to amend the named criteria and not to re-emit them unchanged. Observed here: the conflict was one-sided — one criterion carried a false premise, its partner was faithful to a pinned ruling — and the arithmetic demanded an edit to the faithful one. A contradiction needs a way to name which member is at fault, or a one-sided conflict corrupts a correct criterion on the way out.

**3. There is no reader from a body checklist back into the criteria types.** The sweep consumes generated-criterion values; nothing parses an "## Acceptance criteria" checklist — id, hard/soft, tick state, the graded sha carried inline — into them, and nothing writes one back. Stage 2 needs the read direction and the in-loop tick needs the write direction, and neither exists. (This is the executable core of the checklist-on-body issue on this lane.)

**4. The three-state verdict has no home on the write surface.** The validation record serializes to a stream frame and into the run's criteria artifact; nothing puts a verdict, a blocker stamp or a class marker onto the body checklist. So an `unverifiable`-pending-blocker verdict — which the contract admits and the stage-2 brief requires stamped into the checklist line — cannot be stamped where the criterion lives. This pass had nowhere to write one and only avoided the problem because no criterion in the set took that arm.

**5. The class marker survives only as prose.** On the body the hard/soft classification is a parenthesised word; downstream the class is a typed enum that decides what a failure costs. Two of the graded criteria measure a grep shape standing in for a behaviour and are marked hard — a misclassification the machine currently cannot see, because the marker never becomes a typed value.

Also recorded, as the manual substitution this act had to make: the validator's JUDGMENT half has no standalone entry point over board criteria at all — the refuter template is reachable only inside the workflow's criteria stage, over criteria the same run generated. Its harness half is cleanly drivable standalone and was driven. The stage-2 node needs exactly the missing half: the same contract, pointed at criteria it did not author, on an issue body rather than in a run's own state.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-08-12T06:08:09.039Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-12T06:08:09.022Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"62a86e78-c112-427b-8093-ab65cf915133","body":"[criteria-validation] Stage-2 validation — 2026-08-12 · **PROVISIONAL, pending top-tier re-verification**

**Observed, not theorised. 2026-08-08.** Lane PR 1's loop reported 51/51 accepted. Two independent auditors then refuted it with nine blocking or important findings. The cause is a shape defect in the loop, and it is the most valuable thing this run produced.

**What happened.** The evaluator graded the branch at a six-commit head and accepted. A review-and-fix stage then ran and landed **five more commits**. Nothing graded them. The loop's shape was `execute ⇄ evaluate → review → fix → land`, so the last writer to touch the branch ran *after* the last reader.

**What those ungraded commits did.** Every one of them silently widened a rule someone had deliberately pinned hours earlier:
- a ruling pinned "at most one workflows request per call, never two" — a later commit added a mandatory second confirming probe;
- an acceptance criterion said a failed probe degrades to the longer grace window and "never crashes the call" — a later commit let a retry-exhausted 429 escape instead;
- a ruling pinned `_run_with_exit_codes` as explicitly **out of scope** — a later commit changed it;
- a committed design specified a two-arm predicate and positively excluded a third — a later commit added the third arm;
- the lane's Verification froze `protocols.py`, `test_ralph_workflow.py` and `tests/fakes.py` — later commits changed all three, adding a new port method and a new event.

None of this was malice or sloppiness in the ordinary sense. A review stage does what review stages do: it improves things. The defect is that improvement after grading is indistinguishable from regression, because nobody re-derived anything.

**The invariant to build.** An accept verdict is a statement about a specific sha, not about a branch. So:

1. **Every cross-off records the sha it was graded at.** A cross-off whose recorded sha is not HEAD is not a cross-off — it is a **lapsed claim**, and lapsing is computed, never noticed. This makes staleness arithmetic rather than a thing an auditor has to catch.
2. **No unevaluated commits.** Any stage that writes to the branch — execute, review-fix, a rescued interruption, a human's hand — must be followed by an evaluation before any cross-off stands. Equivalently: the accept verdict is the last thing that touches the branch, or it is not a verdict.
3. **Recorded evidence carries its sha too.** The auditors found roughly ten stale factual claims in PR #42's body: "296 passed" against an actual 313, "`protocols.py` unchanged" against two changes, "the probe fires at most once per call" against a second probe, and a live-verification log sequence that **cannot be produced by the code at HEAD**. All were true when written and all pin to a moved sha. Evidence whose sha is not HEAD is flagged lapsed by the same mechanism.

**The mechanism half, which is F18's implementation and got this wrong too.** This run's loop **copied** each issue's criteria into workflow-private identifiers (`KOD-42/AC-1`) with no link back to the checkbox lines they came from, and then forbade the write-back stage from editing descriptions. So the verdicts had nowhere to land: the evidence went into comments while the `- [ ]` boxes a human actually reads stayed empty. Criteria must be **referenced, not mirrored** — a stable addressable identity per criterion that the tick writes back to. A loop that copies its criteria has created a second source of truth about its own goal, which is the defect this whole board spent a night removing.

Companion to [[F18]]: F18 fixes the cadence of the cross-off, F19 fixes its **validity**. Together: tick as the evaluator passes, stamp the sha, lapse it when HEAD moves, and never let a writer be the last thing before a cross-off.

The audit-side half of this — treating a lapsed cross-off as a first-class finding rather than re-deriving it silently — belongs on KOD-79, which another writer currently owns. The F17 comment above got the causality backwards and is superseded. Recording the correction rather than editing it away, because the wrong version is instructive.

**The founder's ruling:** an issue is Done when its Verification section is demonstrated **in the branch**. Tracking acceptance criteria and then withholding Done until a merge makes the criteria pointless — you merge *once you are done with all of them*, so the merge is the consequence of completion, never its precondition.

**Why the earlier version was wrong, precisely:** it made Done depend on the merge while the merge decision depends on knowing you are done. That is circular. Worse, it drains the board of signal at the one moment the signal is needed: a lane where every criterion passes would show nothing Done, so "are we ready to merge?" becomes unanswerable from the tracker — which is the opposite of the tracker being the progress oracle.

**The corrected transition order:**

1. A criterion is satisfied when demonstrated in the branch that carries the work.
2. All of a sub-issue's criteria demonstrated → the sub-issue is **Done**.
3. All sub-issues Done **and** the lane-level Verification story demonstrated → the fire is **Done**. *This is the signal to merge* — the walker's output that the landing coordinator consumes.
4. Merge.
5. The milestone is crossed.
6. The audit pass re-verifies independently and may reopen with evidence. It grades the **branch**, since that is where the work is — it does not wait for the merge either.

**Consequence for the ambiguous protocol wording.** The v0.2 protocol's *"demonstrated in the landed PR"* reads two ways: "in the PR that lands it" or "after it has landed." The founder's ruling settles it as the former — the PR carrying the work, i.e. the branch. That wording is being corrected on the v0.2 initiative so the two boards do not disagree.

**What survives from the earlier version:** the distinction between the machine's own verdict and an independent one. The audit is still a separate step and a Done that the audit refutes still reopens with evidence. What changed is only that Done is no longer gated on a forge event — it is gated on the work existing and being demonstrated, which is a property of the branch.

Still companion to [[F11]] and [[F16]]: write what is true when it becomes true. The correction is that "the criteria are met" becomes true in the branch, not at the merge.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-08-08T11:48:14.217Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-08T11:48:14.197Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null},{"id":"d1b19d4a-c172-4e29-bfe2-5d6a25036dea","body":"## F17 — the cross-off trigger is the MERGE, not the accept

**Found 2026-08-08 while checking whether KOD-42 was crossable.** The charter's write-back says *"criteria pass → issue Done per the progress protocol"* — i.e. the walker crosses an issue off when its evaluator accepts. The v0.2 progress protocol it claims to execute says something different: *"Done = the issue's Verification section demonstrated in **the landed PR**, which is linked on the issue."*

Those are not the same moment, and the gap is not academic. A lane can be accepted, have a green gate, have its live verification protocol executed with results recorded — all true of KOD-42 right now — and still have its PR closed unmerged, rebased away, or superseded. Crossing off at accept time leaves issues falsely Done with no landed code behind them. That is the precise failure the v0.2 board spent this whole run recovering from, one level down: a claim written before the thing it claims.

**Ruled, to be built here:** the cross-off fires on the **merge**, not the accept. Concretely, three distinct transitions rather than two:

1. **Accepted** — every criterion demonstrated, gate green → the issue moves to In Review and the PR is attached. This is the walker's write-back and it is the machine's own verdict.
2. **Landed** — the PR merges → the issue moves to Done, with the merge commit recorded. This is a forge event, not a judgment, so it is arithmetic.
3. **Audited** — the L7 pass independently re-verifies the accept claims against the merged code and may reopen with evidence. A Done set at step 2 is provisional until step 3 confirms it; a refuted claim reopens.

**Why the ordering matters for the milestone rule.** A milestone is crossed when its fire is Done, and its fire is Done when its sub-issues are resolved. If sub-issues go Done at accept, a milestone crosses on the machine's own say-so with nothing merged — and the initiative's completion condition becomes satisfiable without a single line reaching main.

**Live illustration to build against:** KOD-42 today is demonstrably complete (51/51 across its lane, gate green, live protocol executed and recorded in PR #42's body) and correctly **not** crossed off, because #42 is open. That is the protocol working, not an oversight. The machine graded itself and the rule declines to accept its own green light as sufficient.

Companion to [[F11]] and [[F16]] on this lane — all three are the same discipline from different angles: write what is true when it becomes true, and never earlier.","attachments":[],"createdAt":"2026-08-08T11:45:55.279Z","updatedAt":"2026-08-08T11:45:55.225Z","parentId":null,"resolvedAt":null,"quotedText":null,"author":{"id":"998f68f9-58c0-4c31-bdc8-2b9d8da803a2","name":"Goofy"},"onBehalfOf":null}],"hasNextPage":false}
